<!-- Source: docs-site/index.md -->

# ForeverLM

ForeverLM keeps everything you learn from in one library, and you work on it in **notebooks**: the sources for one piece of work, a chat that reads the ones you tick, and a Studio that makes audio overviews, reports, cards and courses from them. The cards you keep come back for review across every notebook.

## The problem

You read articles and papers. You listen to podcasts and read books. All of this to make sense of the world, but just throwing stuff at the wall and seeing what sticks is not an effective way to remember any of it.

The research is clear: [quizzing yourself is the single most effective way to learn](https://www.hubermanlab.com/episode/optimal-protocols-for-studying-learning). Not re-reading, not highlighting, not summarizing. Actively testing your recall. Explaining it back takes this further: if you can't explain something simply, from scratch, you don't actually understand it. Michael Nielsen makes the deeper point in [Augmenting Long-term Memory](https://augmentingcognition.com/ltm.html): with the right system, remembering something becomes a choice rather than a matter of luck.

Getting that system right is its own problem. In [Memory Machines](https://memory-machines.com/report#1-a-problem-with-two-parts), Ozzie Kirkby and Andy Matuschak find that the hard part isn't working out what you want to remember — the passages readers highlight signal that reasonably well — it's writing questions that still hold up after months of review.

But there's a second problem beyond retention: **tracking all your content**. As Andy Matuschak explores in [How Might We Learn?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MrtNylseFSk), the tools we use for learning are far behind the tools we use for everything else. You consume across dozens of sources and formats, and none of it is connected.

## How ForeverLM fits in

Today, learning and research is fragmented across a stack of disconnected tools: reference managers (Paperpile, Zotero), reading lists (Matter, Pocket), note-taking apps (Notion, Obsidian), and flashcard apps (Anki, Mochi). None of them talk to each other, and none of them were designed for how we actually learn.

ForeverLM brings all your sources into one library. A notebook gathers the ones for one piece of work — a topic, a person's research, a paper to review, a meeting to prepare. A source lives once in the library and can be in any number of notebooks, so the whole library is one search away from inside any of them. You can use Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, or Edison Scientific, or stay inside ForeverLM with the in-app Chat panel.

The workflow is simple:

1. **Collect sources** in [Studio](/studio) — articles, papers, podcasts, books, and more flow in automatically from your browser reading lists, local files, and integrations.
2. **Work in a notebook** — [make a notebook](/studio#notebooks) for what you are working on, add sources from your library, a link, a PDF or a search of the web, and make an audio overview, a report or cards from the ones you tick.
3. **Read, listen, and chat** — use the Reader, [Text to Speech](/text-to-speech), or [in-app Chat](/in-app-chat) to work through the notebook's sources.
4. **Learn through dialogue** — ask your AI to [test you, probe your understanding, and challenge your explanations](/learning-with-mcp) using explain-it-back review and Socratic dialogue.
5. **Remember it** — review the cards you kept, across every notebook, in [Memory](/studio#memory).

For a persistent connection where your AI can search your entire library without dragging, you can optionally [connect an AI assistant](/setup-mcp). MCP traffic passes through ForeverLM-operated Cloudflare infrastructure.

Your knowledge base lives in your private iCloud container. ForeverLM servers do not store your source library, but data you choose to send to AI providers or through the hosted MCP relay follows those connection paths.

<!-- Source: docs-site/why-quizzing.md -->

# Why Quizzing?

## The research

Decades of cognitive science research converge on one finding: **active recall is the most effective way to learn**. Not re-reading, not highlighting, not summarizing. Testing yourself.

This is sometimes called the [testing effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testing_effect) — the finding that retrieving information from memory strengthens that memory far more than passively reviewing it. Andrew Huberman covers the key studies in his [Optimal Protocols for Studying & Learning](https://www.hubermanlab.com/episode/optimal-protocols-for-studying-learning) episode. Andrej Karpathy [recently explored](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2039805659525644595) this same idea in the context of AI-assisted learning.

Explaining it back takes this further: if you can explain a concept simply, from scratch, as if teaching someone else, you understand it. If you can't, you've found your gaps.

## Why not flashcards?

Traditional flashcards (Anki, Mochi) work well for rote memorization — vocabulary, dates, formulas. But they're limited for deeper understanding:

- **Static questions produce static answers.** You end up memorizing the wording of the card rather than understanding the concept.
- **Cards don't adapt.** A flashcard can't probe a gap it doesn't know about.
- **Recognition isn't understanding.** Picking the right answer from a prompt is very different from explaining something from scratch.

AI changes this. An AI assistant can rephrase questions, follow up on weak spots, ask you to explain *why* rather than just *what*, and evaluate your explanations for accuracy and depth. It's the difference between a multiple-choice test and a conversation with a knowledgeable tutor.

We think the best format for AI-powered quizzing is still an open research question. Static flashcards may be a thing of the past — but what replaces them? The explain-it-back review and Socratic dialogue are strong starting points, and we're actively exploring what works best.

As Andy Matuschak explores in [How Might We Learn?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MrtNylseFSk), the tools we use for learning are far behind the tools we use for everything else. ForeverLM is our attempt to close that gap.

## Why not a note-taking app?

There are plenty of great note-taking apps — Notion, Obsidian, Roam. ForeverLM is deliberately not one of them.

Note-taking apps are designed around *capturing and organizing* information. ForeverLM is designed around *tracking sources and testing your understanding* of them. The difference matters:

- **Source tracking, not note management.** ForeverLM tracks what you've read, watched, and listened to — the source material itself, not your notes about it.
- **AI-powered quizzing, not review.** Instead of re-reading your notes, you quiz yourself with an AI that has access to the original source.
- **Understanding over organization.** The goal isn't a perfect knowledge base. It's actually understanding and remembering what you've learned.

Your AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT) already has access to your sources through MCP. That's a better "note-taking" system than any app — it can search, summarize, compare, and quiz you across everything you've saved.

# macOS App

<img src="/screenshots/macos.png" alt="ForeverLM on macOS" style="max-width: 680px; margin: 16px auto; display: block; border-radius: 8px; box-shadow: 0 2px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.12);" />

ForeverLM is a macOS app for tracking your learning sources, planning what to review, listening to articles, and using AI tutors like Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Edison Scientific, or the built-in Chat panel.

You work in **notebooks**. A notebook holds the sources for one piece of work — a topic, a person's research, a paper to review — with a chat that reads the sources you tick and a Studio that makes audio overviews, reports, cards and courses from them. Every source lives once in your library and can be in any number of notebooks, and each window opens in the notebook you last worked in. See [Notebooks](/studio#notebooks).

## Requirements

- macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later
- Apple Silicon or Intel Mac

## Install

[Download the app](https://releases.foreverlm.com/ForeverLM-0.138.1-build210-universal.dmg) — a notarized universal binary that runs on both Apple Silicon and Intel Macs. It checks for updates hourly and at launch, then offers each new version in the sidebar.

Drag ForeverLM into Applications and open it. While the installer is still mounted, ForeverLM asks whether to move it to the Trash; it ejects the installer and moves the downloaded `.dmg` there. **Keep** leaves it alone, and ForeverLM does not ask about that installer again.

The first launch after an update opens a **What's New** sheet with that release's highlights from this changelog — and, if you skipped a few releases, theirs too. **ForeverLM → What's New in ForeverLM…** brings it back at any time.

New versions reach beta testers first. To be one of them, turn on **Settings → General → Updates → Get beta releases**: your Macs are then offered each beta as well as each regular release, whichever is newer, and show the features still in beta (the Canvas and the Atlas for now). The switch follows your account to all of your Macs. Turning it off hides those features again and never moves a Mac back to an older version; it stays on the beta it has until the next regular release passes it. While a Mac runs a beta, **ForeverLM → About ForeverLM** and the version under Settings say so: "Version 0.123.0 Beta (192)".

## First Launch

ForeverLM asks you to **Sign in with Apple** before anything else. Your Apple Account is your ForeverLM account: there is no separate password to create, no card is needed, and the same sign-in works on every device. ForeverLM is free. Signing in starts your 7 free days of MCP, the connection that lets an outside assistant use your library; after that, MCP is $19 paid once (no subscription), in **Settings → Billing**, and the app itself never locks. In the Mac app, Apple's sign-in opens in a sheet inside the app; sign in as you would on any Apple device and choose whether to share or hide your email.

The in-app Chat, quizzes and background AI work run on your own [OpenRouter API key](https://openrouter.ai/keys), billed by OpenRouter at its cost with nothing added; OpenRouter is the provider supported today. ForeverLM adds nothing to it: add the key from the OpenRouter button at the bottom of the sidebar, then pay models at cost or use free models, which cost $0. Connecting Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Grok [over MCP](/setup-mcp) needs no key; it is the one paid part of ForeverLM (7 days free, then $19 once).

After signing in, the **Set up ForeverLM** guide opens over the Studio, one question to a page. After Full Disk Access (below), its AI step is two short pages: **Connect OpenRouter**, then **Pick your models**, where one tap takes the recommended set (chat on an open-weights model run by US hosts, background work on OpenRouter's free models with a cheap backup). **Choose my own** opens the model the chat starts on and the one background work (transcripts, cleanup, metadata) runs on, a free model whose providers may keep what you send or a paid one, and, with a free model, an answer about meetings, which stay on a paid model unless you let them use the free one too, since a meeting's transcript holds private conversations. OpenRouter's privacy settings are in **Settings → AI Usage**. Continuing lets ForeverLM use the key for that work, and **Settings → Background** changes the model later, for text-only work and for multimodal work (work that looks at a figure or a slide), a free model included, and gives any one task a model of its own on the Tasks tab; while meetings are kept off a free model, it names the model they use. The other steps bring your first sources in, one at a time: Apple Podcasts, the browsers whose Reading List ForeverLM reads, where your papers live, then the books, courses, meetings or YouTube you tick, each on a page of its own; the last asks which AI apps you use and adds ForeverLM to each. **Skip this step** moves on, and **Continue later** closes the guide; **ForeverLM → Set Up ForeverLM…** brings it back at any time. The app then opens on the Space, where **New Notebook** starts your first notebook; after that, each window opens in the notebook you last worked in.

## Safari Reading List Access

ForeverLM discovers articles you save to your **Safari Reading List** by reading Safari's bookmarks file. macOS protects that file, so setup asks for access before its first source step, and a later check reports it if access is still missing: open **System Settings** → **Privacy & Security** → **Full Disk Access**, add ForeverLM with the **+** button (macOS does not list it until you do), turn it on, then relaunch the app. Setup, the guide and the empty-library screen all offer a button that takes you there, and setup comes back to the same step after the relaunch.

Without that access, you can still add sources by pasting URLs, dropping PDFs, or saving to the Chrome or Brave reading list.

## Using with AI

Select sources in the Library and [drag them into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, or Edison Scientific](/drag-and-drop) — no setup required.

For a persistent connection where your AI can search your full library without dragging, you can optionally [connect an AI assistant](/setup-mcp). Claude users can [add ForeverLM as a custom plugin](/setup-mcp#claude-custom-connector); it is not in the Claude Directory yet. The [official ChatGPT plugin](/setup-mcp#official-extensions) has been submitted to OpenAI and is in review; custom MCP setup remains available until it is public. Grok users can [add ForeverLM as a custom plugin](/setup-mcp#grok-custom-connector) at grok.com/connectors; it is not in the Grok catalog yet. For always-on access, open Web Studio, choose **MCP** in Chat, and authorize the separate hosted connection. After **MCP ✓** appears, the Mac app and Web Studio can both stay closed.

You can also use [in-app Chat](/in-app-chat) when you want to stay inside ForeverLM. It uses your configured API provider, saves review sessions, and links completed reviews back to sources.

## Key Features

- **Notebooks**: the sources for one piece of work, with its chat and its Studio's audio overviews, reports, cards and courses
- **Library**: every source in one place, managed across the whole window (⇧⌘L)
- **Schedule**: assign sources to days and track review progress
- **In-app Chat**: ask questions and run reviews with your own API provider
- **Memory**: the cards you keep from your sources, drafted for you as you finish them, reviewed across every notebook or one
- **Teams**: a shared library beside your own, stored in its creator's iCloud; share sources, notebooks, Pages and chat transcripts by copy and work a task board together ([Teams](/teams))
- **Text to Speech**: listen to articles and text sources with on-device or cloud TTS
- **Source ingestion**: automatic discovery from browser reading lists, local PDFs, podcasts
- **Drag & drop to AI**: drag sources into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, or Edison Scientific
- **Semantic search**: find sources by concept across your entire library
- **iCloud sync**: all data stored in your private iCloud container, with sync status in Settings

# Web Library

> The web app is being rebuilt around notebooks and is not open to everyone
> yet. Use the [ForeverLM Mac app](https://foreverlm.com/download).

Sign in with the Apple Account that you use for ForeverLM. Web Studio reads and
writes the same CloudKit records as the Mac and iPhone apps: your own library,
and the [team](/teams) libraries you created or joined. In ordinary Web Studio
use, source records and files go directly between your browser and Apple. The
optional always-on MCP connection is the exception described below.

The library switcher works as on the Mac: click your name at the bottom of the
rail and choose **Library**. Web Studio can switch to a team, read its sources,
notebooks, Pages and shared transcripts, and work the task board of a team
notebook. A notebook's **Share** (below) gives its
team's link or has your Mac share it; inviting people by name and removing
members, and sharing anything else into a team, happen on the Mac in this
release.

Press **⌘K** or **⇧⌘P** (Ctrl on Windows and Linux) for the command menu, as on
the Mac and in Codex: one field, "Search chats or run a command". Before you
type it lists your pinned and recent chats and your recent Pages; as you type
it finds places (the Space, Pages, Sites, Courses, Google Drive, Plugins),
chats, notebooks, Pages and Sites, and sources by title. ↑ and ↓ move, Return
opens, Escape closes. Inside a Page, ⌘K still makes a link.

The web app opens on your Space, as the Mac does: **All** lists every notebook
and course beside your Pages, sites and Google Docs, and the Space's search finds
a notebook by its name, summary or topic. **New ▾ › Notebook** asks for nothing:
the notebook opens at once as **New notebook**, and once it holds a source or a
chat, ForeverLM on your Mac names it. A name you type is never replaced. A
notebook's **⋯** has Share…, **Add to Collection** (tick a collection, or make a
new one), **Pin to Sidebar**, Archive and Delete; an archived notebook waits in
**Trash** with **Restore**. With a collection made, the sort and filter menu's
**Group by Collection** shows All under each collection's heading, whose **⋯**
renames or deletes it; this browser remembers the choice. **Courses**, in the
Space's sidebar, shows every course, and a course opens its lessons there. The
Space's lists come newest activity first, a page's **⋯** leads with Codex's
**Rename…**, **Pin** and **Move to Trash**, and a pinned page dragged onto
another in **Pinned** moves there, the same order your Mac shows. ⌘-click (Ctrl
on Windows) or Shift-click rows to choose several, and the bar at the foot of
the list moves them to a space, pins them or puts them in Trash (in Trash,
restores or deletes them). The search in All, Pages and a space finds a page
by what it says as well as by its name; a page this browser has not read yet
is fetched for the search in the background. A space's **⋯** moves it to
**Trash**, where **Restore** brings it back with its pages; Trash keeps
everything until you empty it. **New ▾** also makes an **Image** (a new chat
with "Create an image of" typed) and a page from one of the learning
templates, as on the Mac. The
rail's **Notebooks** comes back to All, and under it are your pinned notebooks
and the six you worked in last, rather than every notebook. A chat's right-click
has **Pin Chat**, **Rename**, **Mark as Unread**, Move to Notebook and **Delete**
(which asks first): a pinned chat leaves the Chats list for **Pinned**, under
your pinned notebooks, the same pins your Mac shows, and dragging one onto
another reorders them. A chat whose reply finished while you had another chat
open shows a dot, as does a notebook holding one, until you open it; these
dots are this browser's own. **Memory** starts a
review of what is due in a chat; **Plugins** lists the plugins a browser can
reach (Google Drive, Slack, Linear, GitHub and Notion) with whether each is
connected, and a plugin's page has its one action: **Manage** for the four read
on the web, **Open Mac App** for Google Drive, whose folders are chosen on the
Mac. Settings has no Plugins, as on the Mac. A notebook opens as one
page with three columns: **Sources** (tick the ones its chats read; a new chat
reads the ticked sources, and a source you add arrives ticked, even one you
unticked before removing it; each notebook it uses context from is a group
below its own sources, whose box puts that notebook's sources into the chats
or takes them out, and **Add a Notebook to Context…** in **Add sources** links
another notebook and puts it in at once), **Chat**, and **Studio**; on a window narrower than
800 pixels they are three tabs, one at a time. A source you open, from
Sources or a citation in the chat, opens in the full Reader (its PDF, page,
video or transcript, with your highlights) beside the chat, in Studio's place;
**×** goes back to Studio. The search at the top of
Sources looks in your library as you type, the notebook's own sources first,
then the rest of your library, where a click reads a source without adding it
and **＋** (or **＋ Add to notebook** in the Reader) adds it. Choose **Web**, or press Return, and your Mac searches the
web for what you typed; the results arrive as a card in Sources, and one your
library already holds is added from your library, never imported twice.
**Add sources** takes a pasted link or DOI, or files from your computer.
Studio lists what the notebook made, each with its kind, how many sources it
was made from and how long ago: its Pages open in the column to read and edit,
and **＋ Page** starts one in the notebook; an audio overview shows its recipe
and script, a walkthrough what it teaches, an explainer its script and a
course (one the notebook follows) its lectures, and they play in the Mac or iPhone app. The notebook's
name, or its **⋯**, opens **Notebook settings**: its name and instructions,
research questions and the rest of its card.
**Share**, at the top right, shows who has the notebook in each team it is in
and gives **Copy Invitation Link**, the link that lets people join that team
and so get the notebook with its sources. A notebook in no team is shared by
your Mac while it is open: it makes a team named after the notebook, moves the
notebook into it and answers with the link. The first time you share, on any device, you confirm
that you have the rights to share these sources.
Studio's **Cards** reviews the notebook's kept cards one at a time: type
your answer and press **Check** (Return), or **I don't know**; ForeverLM checks
your answer against the card with your Card Answer Check model and says
**Right**, **Partly** or **Not quite** with a line on what was missing. The
check's grade is the dark button and Return takes it; the other says **I was
right** or **I was wrong**, and what you choose is recorded, counted the way
the Mac counts it. When the check cannot run, the card says so and you grade
it yourself. It
brings in new cards up to your **New cards each day** (Settings → General →
Memory review on your Mac, 10 by default), counting those you began today in
any notebook; the rest wait for another day, or for **Practice** once nothing
is left for today.

A **mnemonic reading** your Mac made opens from the notebook's Studio: each
chapter's own text with a question after the passage it tests. Answer in your
head, **Show Answer**, then **Forgot** or **Remembered**; either keeps the
question as a card, as on your Mac, and it comes back in the card review on its
schedule. An answered question folds to one line saying when it comes back, and
**Next Question** goes to the next one you have not answered.

Studio makes things too. **Report** writes a briefing, a study guide,
questions for a meeting, feedback on a document or a report of your own into a
Page in the notebook, here in a notebook chat or on your Mac. Written here, each
source is read whole when it fits: 24,000 characters a source, 32,000 in all.
When a source is longer, the dialog names it and offers **Write on your Mac**,
which reads every source whole; a report never reads part of a source. **Deep research** opens a chat that
searches the web. A notebook's empty chat has a **Feynman Technique** chip that asks you to say what you know about the notebook, from memory, then asks about the gaps and fills them in, as on your Mac (see [Inside a notebook](/studio#inside-a-notebook)); reopened on either, it goes on asking. **Audio overview**, **Make cards**, **Mnemonic reading**,
**Course** and **Explainer**, a source's **Walk through on your Mac**, and the Sources
search's **By meaning** and **Web** are done by ForeverLM on your
Mac while it is open and signed in to the same iCloud account: a paid one
shows its price first, and what it makes arrives in the notebook through
iCloud. With your Mac away, those buttons say so and wait.

The workspace around the Space holds your chats, the Reader and your
sources, two side by side at most. The search over your sources reads titles,
authors and links as you type; with words in it, **Search by meaning** (your
Mac) and **Search inside sources** look deeper, and what they find leads the
list. Books, courses, meeting series and YouTube
playlists appear among your sources as collections you expand, with their chapters and
lectures in reading order. Planning your day and scheduling sources happen in
the Mac app.

Chats use the same synced Chat model setting. The browser never holds your
OpenRouter key, so on the web they run on ForeverLM AI: they need a complimentary
account or a ForeverLM balance bought before prepaid balance was retired on
September 25, 2026; otherwise the composer says to chat in ForeverLM on your Mac.
The **+** at the left of the composer also offers Deep Research, on the chat's own model, with
live web search and cited results. Citations into a video, podcast, or
recording show the cited moment (`[2 · 12:34]`) and list it as a chip under the
source, as on the Mac; a slide frame captured from a video lives only on the Mac
that captured it, so Web Studio marks such a picture unavailable.
The web library has no voice conversation. The Chat composer's microphone
dictates: it records until you stop, for up to five minutes, then OpenRouter
transcribes the recording on the Dictation model chosen on your Mac and the
words land in the composer for you to send. The Reader's **Listen** reads a
source aloud, and the pictures Chat draws come from the model in **Settings**
-> **Images**, which lists every image model OpenRouter serves. All three go
through OpenRouter, as on the Mac, and are billed like the web's chat.

Reader progress, read state, notebook membership, and a notebook's ticks sync
back through CloudKit. Add a URL or import a PDF, text, Markdown, HTML, RTF, or
CSV file. Sources can be selected in batches, dragged onto a notebook, edited,
hidden, removed, or restored from Hidden Items, where clicking a hidden source opens
it in the Reader and it stays hidden (a hidden book is listed as its chapters).
Collection actions
cover books, courses, meeting groups, and YouTube playlists. Web-authored chats
and completed reviews also appear in the native chat history.
Notebook open questions can be added, resolved, and reopened on either Mac or
web.

The web library includes synced source metadata and readable text, and the
original PDF or EPUB of a paper, book or course file once your Mac has uploaded
it to iCloud.

Global artifact titles, notebook links, and bounded Markdown bodies sync to Web
Studio. Notepad can edit those bodies and open the existing Chat beside a
selection, carrying the passage and linked sources with it just like the Mac.
A notebook's own workspace files remain Mac-only. Search by meaning uses the Mac's on-device
embedding index, asked while the Mac is open; search by title, author and
link works here without it.

The web app does not host MCP itself: your Mac does while it is open. The
**MCP** control in Chat sets up an always-on connection. It opens a separate
iCloud authorization page so ForeverLM's hosted MCP service receives its own
revocable session instead of borrowing Web Studio's rotating session. After
**MCP ✓** appears, ChatGPT and other connected assistants can use the library
while the Mac app, iPhone app, and browser are all closed. The hosted service
keeps an account-scoped metadata and relationship cache synchronized from your
private iCloud library. It fetches readable source text from iCloud
only when a tool asks for that source and does not cache source files. Reopen
the setup page to disconnect and delete the hosted session and cache.

## In ForeverLM's new iCloud store

The web library reads and writes your library in the
[new iCloud store](/icloud-storage#foreverlms-new-icloud-store) only, the same records
as the Mac and the iPhone. A library your Mac is still uploading opens with what has
arrived so far.

- **Search inside your sources works without your Mac.** **Search inside
  sources**, under the sources' search, finds a word in the text of every source. The first time, the page asks
  whether ForeverLM's hosted assistant connection may link to your iCloud library
  to build the index; say no and it asks your Mac, or, if your Mac is closed,
  searches titles and summaries only. If you use Advanced Data Protection, Apple
  blocks web access to your iCloud data, and the page says so.
- **Papers of any size are here.** Each file is stored in parts, so a large PDF is
  in the web library like a small one.
- **Team notebooks are yours to edit.** A team's notebooks, Pages and chats appear
  as before, and a notebook that was moved into a team is edited in place. Moving a
  notebook into a team from the web asks your Mac to do it.
- **Your own place is private.** Where you got to, your highlights and your cards
  are saved for you alone, as on the Mac.

## Teams

The library switcher, **Library** in the account menu at the bottom of the left
navigation, lists My Library and every team you own or have joined. Web Studio
reads a team the same way the Mac does: a team is one CloudKit zone, read from
your private database when you created it and from the shared database when you
were invited, so sources,
notebooks, Pages, and shared chats appear in that team's library. Chats shared
into a team are read-only transcripts. Every notebook's settings carry a task
board; in a team notebook a task can be assigned to a member, and members with
read-only access see the library and the board without edit controls.

A notebook's **Share** gives its team's invitation link, or asks your Mac to
share it into a new team named after it. Inviting people by name, removing
members, and sharing anything else into a team happen in the Mac app;
CloudKit's web framework has no zone-wide sharing sheet.

The first load may take longer for a large library. The browser keeps an
account-scoped local mirror and requests only CloudKit changes on later visits.
Use the refresh button to sync immediately; returning to the tab also refreshes
after a short cooldown.

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/studio.md -->

# Studio

<img src="/screenshots/macos.png" alt="ForeverLM Studio chat home with the source library" style="max-width: 760px; margin: 16px auto; display: block; border-radius: 8px; box-shadow: 0 2px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.12);" />

Studio is ForeverLM's window, and you work in it in a **notebook**: the
sources for one piece of work — a topic, a person's work, a paper to review, a
meeting to prepare — with a chat that reads them and a Studio column that makes
things from them. Your library holds every source once. A notebook only points at the
sources it uses, so one paper can be in any number of notebooks, removing it
from a notebook never deletes it, and the whole library stays one search away
from inside any notebook. The cards you keep and review span every notebook
([Memory](#memory)).

## Notebooks

### Your notebooks in the Space

The Space is ForeverLM's home. A window opens in the notebook you last worked
in on this Mac (opened, chatted in, or added a source to); with no notebook
yet, or when that notebook was archived, deleted or belongs to another
library, the window shows the Space's **All** list. **Spaces** in the rail, the
rail's **Notebooks** heading, ⌘P (View → Space), **Close Notebook** and **‹** at
the top of an open notebook take you there too.

**All** lists every notebook and course beside your pages, sites and
canvases. Pictures are listed under **Images**, not in **All**. A notebook shows its cover, or its emoji on its own soft colour (an
emoji at the start of the title is its icon; without one, ForeverLM picks one
that fits the title, the same on every device), dated by when you last worked
in it. Click a notebook to open it; drag a source or a course onto it to add
it. Its **⋯** and right-click menu have **Open in Other Window**, **Share…**,
**Add to Collection ▸**, **Pin**, **Draw Cover With ▸**, **Archive**, **Merge
into Notebook…** and **Delete Notebook…**. The Space's search finds a notebook
by its title, description or topic, and **New ▸ Notebook** makes one.

**Collections** group notebooks, as in Gemini Notebook. **Add to Collection ▸**
in a notebook's menu puts it in a collection (a notebook can be in several) or
makes a **New Collection…**. Once you have one, the list's sort and filter
menu offers **Group by Collection**: All shows each collection's notebooks
under its heading, and everything else last. A heading's **⋯** renames or
deletes the collection; deleting it leaves its notebooks where they are.
Collections follow your account to your other Macs, the web app and the
iPhone, where the notebook list can show one collection at a time.

**Archived notebooks** are in the Space's **Trash**, after any pages and sites
you put there. Point at one for **Restore**, or use its menu to open, merge or
delete it. **Empty Trash** leaves them alone.

A new notebook opens at once, with nothing to fill in.
It reads **New notebook** until you add a source or start a chat; then
ForeverLM names it and writes the line on its card. Once you rename it,
ForeverLM never renames it again.

### Inside a notebook

A notebook fills the window in three columns, as in Gemini Notebook:

| Column | What it holds |
|--------|---------------|
| **Sources** (left) | ‹ back to the Space, the notebook's name (click it to rename) and its **⋯** menu. **Sources** with **Add sources**, one field that searches the notebook, your whole library and the web (see [Searching for sources](#searching-for-sources)), "8 of 12 in chat" with **Select all**, then its sources by type, then a group for each notebook it uses context from. Each source has a box: ticked sources are what the notebook's chats read and what its Studio makes things from. Click a source to read it beside the chat; its **⋯** has **Open**, **Open in Other Window** and **Remove from Notebook**. An empty notebook offers **Suggested from your library**, each row one click from joining, and **Add all**. Drop PDFs from Finder or a browser on the column to import them as papers into the notebook |
| **Chat** (center) | The notebook's chat, and beside it one document: the Reader, a Page, a Site, an animation, a course's page, the Browser, Memory, a second chat or a picture from the chat (**Open beside** on a figure). The Reader is the full one: a paper with its figures, a video with its transcript, a book, a web page. A new document replaces the one beside the chat; the divider between them drags, and each has its **×** |
| **Studio** (right) | **Share** at its top right ([Sharing a notebook](/teams#sharing-a-notebook)), then what you can make from the ticked sources, and everything the notebook made |

An empty notebook chat shows the notebook's name and description, and, once it
has sources, **Suggest questions**, **Quiz me on it** and **Feynman Technique**,
then the notebook's latest chats; with no sources it offers **Add sources**. The chat's **⋯** has
**Chats in This Notebook ▸**: **New Chat** starts a chat in the notebook the
window holds, reading its ticked sources, and the notebook's chats follow. A
chat filed in a notebook opens in that notebook, and a library chat (one in no notebook) leaves it. Coming back
to a notebook reopens the chat you last had open in it.

**Feynman Technique** is the notebook's way to find out what you know, built for
learning by pictures. Press its chip, or say in the notebook's chat that you want
to do the Feynman Technique, and a new chat opens asking you to say what you know
about the notebook, in your own words, from memory, in whatever order it comes.
The tutor reads the ticked sources privately and never explains first. It answers
with a picture from your sources, a figure, diagram or slide, and one short
prompting question about it, aimed at the biggest gap: a term you didn't define, a
step you skipped, a claim with no evidence, a mechanism you waved through or a part
of the subject you never mentioned. There are no paragraphs or lists. When
something you say is wrong it shows the picture and asks a question that lets you
notice. When you don't know, or a second try still misses, it fills the gap with
the picture that settles it and a line on where to look, names the source and
where it comes from, and asks you to say it back. Once what you say holds
together, it asks for the whole subject as one picture you could sketch, then for
the assumptions and limits. It goes on until you stop. The chat is kept as a
[review](/in-app-chat#reviews), and reopened later, on this Mac or another, it
goes on probing.

Following a link never closes what you read it in: a citation or a Page's
source opens the Reader beside the chat, and the Reader's **Back to** control,
named after what it replaced (a Page, a Site, Memory, …), brings that back in
one click. In the Reader's **⋯** menu, **Add to** and the notebook's name
(**Add to “Bioelectricity”**) files the source you are reading into the
notebook the window holds.

When a paper opens beside the chat in a narrow window, Sources folds to a
strip with an icon for each source, and Studio stays; if there is still no
room, Studio folds to a strip of Share and its outputs, and then the rail
steps aside for that window until it widens again. A strip's top button
brings its column back. The **Notebook** menu holds **Add Sources…** (⇧⌘I),
**Show/Hide Sources** (⌃⌥⌘S), **Show/Hide Studio**, **Make ▸** (the Studio's
tiles), **New Note**, **Rename Notebook…** and **Close
Notebook**. Two windows can hold two notebooks; each keeps its own.

The notebook's **⋯** (beside its name) has **Add Sources…**, **Add a Notebook
to Context**, **Think First ▸**, **Rename Notebook…**, **Unpin from Sidebar** or **Pin to Sidebar**, **Archive
Notebook** (**Restore Notebook** on an archived one), **Share…**, **Share with Team ▸**,
**Merge into Notebook…**, **Open in Other Window**, **Close Notebook** and
**Delete Notebook…**.

On the iPhone, Home is the list of your notebooks, and a notebook has
**Sources**, **Chat** and **Studio** tabs, with **Share** beside its **⋯**.
The [Web Library](/web-library) opens notebooks the same way.

### The Studio column

The Studio's tiles make something from the notebook's ticked sources. Each
asks first — options, the sources it reads, and the price where there is one —
and makes on the second press:

- **Audio overview**: a spoken overview of the sources, read in one narrator's
  voice (your text-to-speech voice), as a **Deep dive**, a **Brief** or a
  **Critique**, at a length you pick, with an optional focus. It plays in the
  window's player.
- **Cards**: the notebook's cards ("42 kept · 6 due · 9 to check"),
  **Practice**, **Make Cards…** and **Open in Memory** (see [Memory](#memory)).
- **Report**: **Briefing**, **Study guide**, **Questions for a meeting**,
  **Feedback on a document** or **Custom…**, written into a Page in the
  notebook. Each claim in it links to the passage of the source it rests on,
  and the Page ends with the sources it was made from.
- **Video overview**: a short video of the ticked papers and articles. You are
  asked the price first; the film is made in the background, and when it is
  done it joins the notebook's sources, is listed under its outputs, and plays
  in the Reader. With no paper or article ticked there is nothing to film from.
  **Make ▸ Add Video File…** brings in a video you already have, such as one
  downloaded from Gemini Notebook (MP4, M4V or MOV); it has no transcript, and
  importing the same file again adds nothing new.
- **Deep research**: a [Deep Research](/in-app-chat#deep-research) chat in the
  notebook, reading the ticked sources and waiting for your question.
- **Course**: a course-planning chat reading the ticked sources (see
  [Generating a course](/courses#generating-a-course)).
- **Explainer**: pick one of the ticked papers, articles, podcast episodes,
  videos or meetings for its spoken [explainer](#explainers).
- **Add note** (floating at the foot of the column): a new Page in the
  notebook, open beside the chat.

Below the tiles, **Outputs** lists what the notebook made under its **Cards**
row, newest first by when each was made: audio overviews, reports and other
Pages, mnemonic readings, Sites, animations, pictures, videos, the courses the
notebook follows, and the walkthroughs, explainers and narrations of its own
sources (a walkthrough belongs to every notebook that holds its source). This
is the one list of a notebook's pictures, animations, audio overviews,
videos, walkthroughs and narrations. A picture's **⋯** has **Rename…**,
**Add to Notebook ▸** (which moves it, since a picture lives in one
notebook), **Copy Image**, **Copy Prompt**, **Show in Finder** and **Move to
Trash**, and you can drag it out as a file. Click a narration to open its
source in the Reader and play it. Each says what it is, how many sources it was made from
and when ("Briefing · 6 sources · 1 hour ago"), with a dot until you open it
on this Mac. A report, an audio overview or a mnemonic reading being written
shows its stage and **Stop**; an audio overview plays from its row. Click an output to open it
beside the chat; its **⋯** has **Open**, **Open in Other Window**,
**Rename…** for a Page, Site or animation, **Prompt and Sources** (what it was
made to and from, each source a click from the Reader) and, for a Page, Site
or animation, **Remove from Notebook**. In an archived
notebook, or a team notebook you can only view, the tiles that would file
something into it are off; Cards stays on.

### Searching for sources

The Sources column's field, **Search your library and the web**, has
**Library**, **Web** and **PubMed** under it.

- **Library** answers as you type: the notebook's own matching sources under
  **In this notebook**, then **In your library**, sources from the rest of
  your library with a **+** that adds one to the notebook. Clicking one opens
  it in the Reader beside the chat without adding it. Below them, **Search the
  web for “…”** and **Search PubMed for “…”** take your words there.
- **Return** searches the web for your words (from **Library** too) or runs
  the **Web** or **PubMed** search you chose. A web search uses your model and
  is priced like a chat turn, and PubMed is free. The results arrive as a card
  at the top of the column: how many it
  found and how many your library already holds, the first three with why
  each fits, **N more**, **Add N** for the ticked ones, and **×** to put the
  card away.
- **N more** widens the column to the whole list, with a box for each result,
  **↗** to open its page beside the chat, **Select all**, **Add** and
  **Research this deeply** (a Deep Research chat in the notebook with your
  words typed). A result your library already holds joins the notebook as it
  is, never imported twice. **‹ Sources** goes back.

### Adding sources

**Add sources** (in the Sources column, the **⋯** menu, an empty chat, or
⇧⌘I) opens a sheet:

- One field, **Search your library or paste a link**. With
  nothing typed it shows **Suggested from your library**. A search finds
  sources by title, author, text and meaning; tick rows and press **Add N**,
  or **Add all N** (above ten it asks first), or a row's **+** on its own. A
  pasted link or DOI shows **Add link**, which adds the page to your library
  and the notebook in one step; a page the library already holds only joins
  the notebook. **Upload PDF…** imports PDFs from disk as papers in the
  notebook.

The web and PubMed are searched from the Sources column's own field (see
[Searching for sources](#searching-for-sources)).

### The rail

The navigation rail is a narrow strip of icons: **Home**, which opens a new chat
with your notebooks and chats beside it (in a notebook window it leaves the
notebook; the notebook's row brings it back), then **Spaces**,
**Memory**, **Library** and **Plugins**, and at its foot the calendar glyph that opens
today's schedule (see [Layout](#layout)) and your account. Each icon can be
hidden from its own menu and brought back with **Show in Sidebar**; **New chat**
is a row of the sidebar beside a chat, not an icon.

To keep a place one click away, drag its row from the Space's sidebar
(**Pages**, **Notebooks**, **Courses**, **Google Drive** and the rest) onto
the strip, or tick it under the strip's **⋯ › Show in Sidebar**. It stays
under a short line as its icon alone. Drop a place on a kept icon to put it
above that one, drag a kept icon up or down to reorder, and right-click it
for **Remove from Sidebar**.

While anything that costs money runs in the background, a grey OpenRouter
logo shows in the strip; click it for **Running in the background**: each
narration, automatic audio, explainer video, mnemonic reading, scheduled task
run and assistant job, and every paid step ForeverLM takes on its own, such as
Text-to-Speech Preparation, Paper Metadata, a recording's transcription or a
notebook's cover, each with **✕** to stop it. A chat you are typing in is not
listed; it has its own Stop. Stopping a step stops it for every source, since
its queue would otherwise move on to the next one. A step that runs on its
own, and automatic audio, then waits under **Stopped**, on every Mac of your
account, until you press **Resume**; what you ask for yourself, such as
Listen, still runs. A step you asked for, such as a report, is only stopped,
and asking again runs it.

Beside a chat or the Reader, outside a notebook, a sidebar joins the strip:
**New chat** and **Browser** at the top, then **Notebooks**, which opens the
Space's All list, where every notebook is (its right-click menu also opens
**Courses** and the Space, here or beside what you are viewing). Under it,
**Pinned**, the notebooks you pinned, and **Recent**, the last six you worked
in, plus the notebook this window last had open. A notebook's row opens it in
this window and shows its chats, the chevron shows or hides them, and **+** on
hover starts a chat in it. Its menu has **Open in Other Window**, **Pin to
Sidebar** or **Unpin from Sidebar**, **Draw Cover With ▸**, **Archive
Notebook**, **Share…**, **Share with Team ▸** and **Delete Notebook…**. Then
**Chats**, the library's own chats, whose **+** (on hover, or **New Library
Chat** on its right-click menu) starts a library chat; a chat's
**Move to Notebook ▸** files it in a notebook. **Home**, the first icon on the
strip, brings this sidebar back with a new chat beside it. The Space lists
and starts no chats. "Plan your day?" and **Cards to
check** wait at the foot of this sidebar, or in the window's corner where it is
not showing.

Chats work as Codex's do. A chat's menu (right-click, or its **⋯** on hover)
starts with **Pin Chat**, **Rename…**, **Mark as Unread** and **Hide**, then
**Move to Notebook ▸** and where it opens, and ends with **Delete…**, which
asks first. A pinned chat leaves its list for **Pinned**, under your pinned
notebooks, on every Mac and on the web; drag one pinned chat onto another to
reorder them. When a reply finishes while its chat is not on screen in any
window, the chat's row shows a dot until you open it, and a folded notebook
holding such a chat shows one too (its menu has **Mark All as Read**). The
dots are this Mac's own. In an open chat, click its title to rename it; its
**⋯** has **Pin Chat**, **Rename…** and **Hide** too.

The bell above the account is **Activity**, the one place for what waits on
you, as Codex's is: the unread chats (a click opens one) and the ones still
running, a teammate's request for a source you hold (**Share** or
**Decline**, and **Share All** when there are several), a plugin to reconnect
(**Reconnect** opens its page in Plugins), and the corner cards, "Plan your
day?" and **Cards to check** among them. The bell wears a dot while anything
in it is unread, never a number; right-click an item for **Mark as Read** or
**Mark as Unread**, or use **Mark All as Read**. A card's ✕ in the corner
tucks it into the bell, and what you marked read stays read after you quit,
so a card stays out of the corner until it has something new to say.

Inside a notebook only the strip stays, so the notebook's three columns have
the window. A rail you hid stays hidden.

### The command menu and keyboard shortcuts

Press **⌘K** or **⇧⌘P** (View → Command Menu) for the command menu, as in Codex: one field,
"Search chats or run a command". Before you type it offers Quick actions (New
Chat, New Page, Plan the Day in Chat, Today's Review, Keyboard Shortcuts), your
pinned and recent chats and your recent Pages. As you type it finds commands,
places (the Space, Pages, Sites, Courses, Memory, the Library, Plugins and the
rest), chats, notebooks, Pages and Sites, sources (by title at once, then by
what is inside them) and Settings panes, grouped and best match first. ↑ and ↓
move, Return opens, Escape or a click beside it closes. A command that has a key
shows it at the end of its row.

**Help → Keyboard Shortcuts** (⌘/) lists every key the app has. The ones that
follow Codex:

| Keys | What they do |
|------|--------------|
| ⌘K or ⇧⌘P | Command menu |
| ⌘/ | Keyboard shortcuts |
| ⌘[ / ⌘] | Back and forward through the places the window showed (a course, the Atlas or a plugin's page keeps its own ⌘[ while you are in it) |
| ⌃⌘S or ⇧⌘S | Show or hide the sidebar |
| ⌘N or ⇧⌘O | New chat (a new window is ⌃⌘N) |
| ⌥⌘N | Quick chat (the Quick Assistant panel) |
| ⇧⌘[ / ⇧⌘], ⌃⇧Tab / ⌃Tab | Previous and next chat in the sidebar |
| ⌘1 – ⌘9 | Go to the chat at that place in the sidebar, pinned chats first |
| ⌥⌘1 – ⌥⌘6 | Open one of the chats started most recently |
| ⌥⌘R, ⌥⌘P, ⇧⌘U, ⌥⌘L | Rename, pin or unpin, mark as unread, copy the link of the chat on screen |
| ⌥⌘S | Side chat about the whole conversation, as `/side` |
| ⌥⌘A | Next unread chat |
| ⇧⌘A | Hide the chat on screen (Codex's Archive) |
| ⇧Esc | Mark all chats as read |
| ⌃⇧M or ⌃⌘M | The chat's model picker, recent models on top |
| ⌘F, ⌘G, ⇧⌘G | Find in a chat, next, previous |

The **Chat** menu holds these, New Chat is in **File**. ForeverLM's own keys:
⇧⌘K Open Chat (chat about the Reader's selection, else the composer), ⌘R Open
Reader, ⌘P Space, ⇧⌘L Library, ⌘D Plan the Day in Chat, ⇧⌘D Daily Notes, ⇧⌘B
the Pomodoro timer, ⇧⌘I Add Sources… in a notebook, ⌃⌥⌘S Show/Hide Sources, ⌃⌘A
the Atlas and ⌥⇧⌘S Save Canvas Version (both beta). Open Chat was ⌘K, a new
window ⌘N, Add Sources… ⇧⌘A, Show/Hide Sources and Save Canvas Version ⌥⌘S and
the Atlas ⌥⌘A until Codex's keys took them.

On the web, ⌘K or ⇧⌘P opens the same menu over places, chats, notebooks, Pages
and sources ([Web library](./web-library)).

### Plugins

**Plugins** — the rail's grid icon under Library, or View → Plugins — is
where every plugin lives, as in Codex: the built-in ones (X, YouTube, Google
Drive, Calendar, Slack, Linear, GitHub, Notion) and then yours (the meeting
plugins and the ones you built), each with what it reads and **Connected**,
**Not connected** or **Reconnect needed**. Search narrows the list by name.
Click a plugin to open its page in the same place, where you connect it,
choose what it may read and disconnect it; **‹ Plugins** (or ⌘[) goes back.
Like the Library it is a pane with its **×**, **Open Beside** and **Open in
Other Window**, and in a notebook window it leaves the notebook. Settings
has no Plugins. See [Plugins](/external-plugins).

### The Library

**Library** — the rail's row or View → Library (⇧⌘L) —
spreads the whole library across the window for managing it: every source
type, search and filters, each row with chips for the notebooks it is in (a
click opens that notebook) and when it was added. Select two or more rows for
a bar: "N selected", **Add to Notebook ▸**, **New Notebook with N Sources…**,
**Mark Read** or **Mark Unread**, **Hide**, **Remove…**, and × to clear the
selection. Opened from inside a notebook, its top line starts with **‹** and
the notebook's name, which opens it again. A source
clicked here opens in the Reader beside the list.

The Library is also where every source gets its cards. Each row says how many
cards the source has, quietly at its end ("3 cards", "To check", or nothing
yet), and the **No Cards** pill beside the search lists the sources in the tab
that have none, with their count. Under the pointer a row offers **Make
Cards**, which opens the Make Cards sheet for that source (**Make More Cards**
once it has some), and **Not Worth Keeping**, which removes the source as
**Remove** does, with the same Undo; both are on the row's right-click menu
too, where **Make Cards** takes a whole selection. With **No Cards** on, **Make
Cards for 10** at the head makes cards for the first ten sources still waiting
together, so the cards can link the ideas they share. The goal is at least one
card for each source, and every source worth its weight. Team copies, hidden
and paywalled sources, and sources without text are never counted as missing
cards. Assistants read the same list with `list_source_card_coverage`.

To have the library beside what you are doing, drag the rail's **Library**
row to an edge of the window, or choose **Open Beside** on its
right-click menu. It docks as a pane next to your chat, a Page or a canvas
and draws the compact list, with the same tabs, search and row menus; drag a
source from it into a chat, or onto a canvas. Close it with its ×.

### Pages, Goals and Not in a Notebook

The Space holds what you keep working on beyond one notebook, one place per
kind in its sidebar under **New page**: **Notebooks**, **Courses**,
**Pages**, **Sites**, **Canvases** (a beta feature, tagged **Beta**), **Images**
and **Google Drive**, then **Pinned**, **Recents**, your **Spaces** and, at the
foot, **Trash**. The notebook filter beside the team filter shows **All
Notebooks**, one notebook, or what is **Not in a Notebook**. A Page's or Site's card has **Add to Notebook ▸**, with
the notebooks that hold most of its sources first under **Suggested**, and
**Remove from** the notebook it is in. A Page or Site also has a **Notebooks**
checklist in the menu of its own pane.

Everything else you make belongs to one notebook and is listed only in that
notebook's [Studio](#the-studio-column): pictures, animations, audio
overviews, mnemonic readings, videos, walkthroughs and narrations. A mnemonic
reading also shows in its notebook's own Pages list, where it opens; one you
made from the Reader outside any notebook stays in the Space's **Pages**.
Walkthroughs, explainers and narrations ride their source: they are in every
notebook that holds it, and **Walk Through** and **Listen** in the Reader's
⋯ menu reach them too. A picture drawn for a walkthrough or a quiz is in no notebook
and shows where it is used.

#### Working in the Space

The Space's lists come newest activity first, as Codex's do; the sort and
filter menu still offers **Date Created** and **Name**, and opening a page
never moves it. A row's **⋯** and right-click start with Codex's own
**Rename…**, **Pin** and **Move to Trash**, then **Share…**, **Copy ▸** and
**Download as Markdown**, then **Open in Other Window**; ForeverLM's own
(**Add to Chat**, the canvas items, **Add to Notebook ▸**, **Move to Space ▸**,
subpages, **Share with Team ▸**, **Hide**) follow after a divider. Every
**Recents** row has **Remove from Recents** on its menu, and every space in
the sidebar has a **⋯** under the pointer. Pinned pages, canvases and lists
share one order: drag a pinned row onto another to move it there.

To act on several things at once, **⌘-click** rows or cards to choose them,
or **⇧-click** to take in a run; while anything is chosen a plain click
chooses too. A bar at the foot of the list says how many and offers **Move to
Space ▸**, **Pin** and **Move to Trash** (in Trash, **Restore** and **Delete
Forever…**), with **Select All**, and **×** lets them all go; the right-click
of a chosen row offers the same. Images are chosen one at a time.

**New ▾** on **All** and on a space, and **New page**'s **⋯** in the sidebar,
also make an **Image** (a new chat with "Create an image of" typed, ready for
you to say what to draw) and a page from a **template**: **Reading Notes**,
**Literature Review**, **Lecture Notes** or **Weekly Learning Log**, each a
page with its headings, filed in the space you are in.

A space's **⋯** has **Move to Trash**: the space leaves the sidebar, its pages
stay in **All**, and **Trash** lists it with **Restore** (the space comes back
with its pages) and **Delete Forever…**. Things stay in Trash until you empty
it, as Trash says at its head; select several there to restore or delete them
together.

The search at the head of **All**, **Pages**, a space or a team's space finds
a page by what it says as well as by its name: every word you type, anywhere
in the page, in any case and with or without accents. The magnifier at the
top of the Space's sidebar searches every place at once: it opens **All**
with its search ready.

Goals and Ideas have no place of their own in the Space since 2026-10-10: ask
the chat ("what are my goals?", "what are my ideas?") and it lists them, and
`/goal` sets a goal. A list of goals or of ideas you want to keep in view is a
Space item of its own (**New ▸ Goals List** or **Ideas List**).

#### Speaking to a canvas

On a canvas (beta, Mac), hold **S** and say what to change, then let go: "put
these three papers together under Mitophagy", "move the PINK1 note to the
left", "connect this to the Parkin paper", "take the reviews off", "add my
paper on Drp1 next to it". Tap **S** instead, or choose **Speak to the
Canvas** in the canvas's menu, to talk until you pause. The canvas changes
as the answer arrives, and a small bar at its foot says what it heard and
what it did; its **×** or **Esc** stops it. Its **Undo**, or one **⌘Z**, takes
the whole request back. "Move the Methods region down" moves the region with
its cards, and "add my papers on NAD below the Mitophagy region" or "write a
note saying fission comes first between the two regions" sets things down
exactly there.
What a request changed is selected afterwards, so the next can say "now put
these in a row" or "colour them blue". Ask it questions too: "what connects
these?", "what's missing in this group?" or "break this paper down" start
**Ask** on those cards (or on a region's: "what's missing in the NAD region?"), and
when its suggestions come back, "keep the first two" or "get rid of those" keeps or
sets them aside. "Open the Parkin note" opens it beside the canvas.
Your words show in the bar while you say them (heard on your Mac, macOS 26 or
later); when you let go, your **Dictation** model (**Settings → Speech-to-Text**,
the one chat uses) writes them out properly, and the canvas acts on those. The
bar then lists each step as it happens: what it is doing, what it did, and why a
step could not be done. The
changes are made by the **Canvas Voice** model under **Settings → Background
→ Tasks**, which starts on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, the fastest model in
ForeverLM's tests (about half a second to the first change); choose another
there.

### Courses and notebooks

A course lives in no notebook: it is listed in the Space's **All** and under its **Courses**.
Opening one shows its page where you are, and inside a notebook, beside the
chat. A notebook can follow a course, so its sources and every lecture the
course gains join it. A course's **⋯** has **Make Study Notebook**, **Link to
Notebook ▸** and **Unlink from** each notebook that follows it, and its page
says "Linked to" them under its title. See
[Courses](/courses#courses-and-their-notebooks).

### Uses context from, pinning, merging, archiving

These live on the notebook's **⋯** and its card:

- **Uses context from** links other notebooks, its context notebooks, without
  copying sources or nesting one notebook in another. The link is directional
  and one level deep. A context notebook's sources reach this notebook's chats
  only once you put it in: each shows under the notebook's own sources as a
  group, "From \<name\> · N sources", whose box puts it into the chats, or
  takes it out. A source you unticked in it stays unticked when it comes
  back in, and its box shows a dash until you tick it again, which ticks
  them all. Unfold it to tick or untick its sources one by one.
  **Add a Notebook to Context** in the **Add sources** menu (or the
  notebook's **⋯**) links a notebook and puts it in at once; the group's
  **×**, **Take Out of Context**, unlinks it. What the notebook's Studio
  makes reads only its own sources.
- **Instructions** guide every chat in the notebook; the **Description** is
  the short line on its card. The Mac has no settings sheet for a notebook
  since 2026-10-04: its instructions, description, research questions and
  linked GitHub repository are changed in **Notebook settings** in the [Web
  Library](/web-library), or by an assistant over MCP (`update_notebook`).
- **Pin to Sidebar** keeps a notebook under **Pinned** in the rail;
  **Unpin from Sidebar** takes it off and nothing else. A
  notebook without a row in the rail has its chats under **Chats**. Pinning
  syncs to your other Macs.
- **Merge into Notebook…** folds a notebook into another: you pick the one it
  goes **Into** and the merged notebook's name, and its sources (a source in
  both is kept once), chats, open questions, notes, Goals, tasks, Pages,
  courses, scheduled tasks, ideas' links, directions and files move before it
  is deleted (a file whose name both held lands under *From \<merged
  notebook\>*). Notebooks in different libraries do not merge. Over MCP the
  same is `merge_notebooks`.
- **Archive Notebook** retires a notebook; the Space's **Trash** lists
  archived notebooks, each with **Restore**, and an archived notebook opens to
  be read. **Delete Notebook…** asks first: its Goals go with it, you choose
  whether its chats stay in **Chats**, its folder's files move to the Trash,
  and its sources stay in your library.

### Importing a Gemini Notebook

A notebook from Gemini Notebook (called NotebookLM until July 2026) comes in as
a ForeverLM notebook.

1. Open ForeverLM's browser, choose the **Library** profile, and sign in to
   Google. Signing in to your own web browser doesn't count, because ForeverLM
   reads the notebook with the sign-in made inside the app.
2. Paste the notebook's link (`notebook.google.com/notebook/…`; a
   `notebooklm.google.com` link works too) into a notebook's **Add sources**, or
   ask your AI assistant to run `import_gemini_notebook` with it.

The notebook it makes takes the Gemini notebook's title, and a notebook of
yours that already has that title is reused; a pasted link opens it in that
window once it lands. Into it go:

- **Sources.** A web page or YouTube video comes in by its address, the way a
  pasted link does, so a paper's page brings its PDF. A Google Doc is linked in
  Pages. Pasted text, an uploaded file or a PDF comes in as an article holding
  the text the notebook keeps for it, word for word.
- **Chats.** Each chat is filed in the notebook as a chat, not a review, so
  its sources are not marked reviewed. It is linked to the notebook's sources
  and drawn on the day's log at the hours it ran.
- **Notes.** Each note, and each written report from the notebook's Studio,
  becomes a Page in the notebook.

Audio and video overviews, flashcards, quizzes, mind maps and apps stay in
Gemini Notebook, and the import lists each one it left there. Importing the
same notebook again adds only what is new: a chat that went on since is
brought up to date, and a Page is never overwritten, so a note you have edited
keeps your edits.

### Teams

A team is a second library several people share, stored in its creator's
iCloud. Click your name at the foot of the rail: the account menu's
**Library** row names the library that is open and switches between **My
Library** and your teams. Switching reloads Sources, notebooks, Pages and Chats
for that library and leaves the rest of the Studio unchanged.

Source rows, notebook rows and a notebook's **⋯**, Page menus and chat rows in
My Library carry **Share with Team ▸**, and a notebook's **Share** invites
people to it in one step ([Sharing a notebook](/teams#sharing-a-notebook)). A
notebook shared into a team you own moves there; anything else is copied into
the team and the original stays where it is ([Sharing into a
team](/teams#sharing-into-a-team)). A paper two members both share is one team
record. A notebook's task board is in the [Web Library](/web-library), and in a
team notebook its tasks can be assigned to members. Reading progress, review
results, highlights and the Schedule stay private to each member. See
[Teams](/teams).

## Layout

Outside a notebook, the window has the navigation rail and a center workspace
of up to two resizable panes. The library is one of those panes: drag the
rail's **Library** row to an edge to dock it beside another.

| Panel | What it does |
|-------|-------------|
| **Navigation** (left) | **Home** (a new chat, with your notebooks and chats beside it), **Spaces**, **Memory** (where today's cards wait) and **Library**, and at the foot the calendar glyph for today's schedule from the Mac's Calendar; beside a chat or the Reader, **New chat**, **Browser**, **Notebooks** with your pinned and recent notebooks and their chats, and your library's own **Chats** ([The rail](#the-rail)) |
| **Library** | The whole library, organized by type, across the window for managing it or docked beside another pane ([The Library](#the-library)) |
| **Reader** | Displays the selected source: web article, PDF, video, or transcript |
| **Chat** | In-app source-grounded chat and review sessions |
| **Memory** | Your cards across every notebook ([Memory](#memory)) |
| **Day** | Your calendar and what you actually did on a day — the papers read, episodes heard, chats had and Pages written — on one clock. Open it from the **Today** menu or the calendar glyph |
| **Space** | Your notebooks, chats and courses, and your Pages, Sites, Canvases, Images and Google Docs across every notebook, one place per kind in its sidebar, with **Trash** for what you put away and your archived notebooks; with a filter for one notebook or for what is **Not in a Notebook**. A notebook opens across the window ([Inside a notebook](#inside-a-notebook)). Pages and Sites also open in a pane of their own: **Open Pages Beside** or **Open Sites Beside** on the row's right-click menu, or drag the row to an edge of the window |

Click a navigation item to open it in the current pane. Hover it and choose the
split icon to open it beside what you are viewing. Inside a notebook, Memory,
a source or an artifact opens beside the notebook's chat instead; Spaces and
Library leave the notebook, and its row in the rail opens it again.

Drag any saved chat from the navigation rail to the left or right edge of the
workspace to open it as a second, independently interactive Chat pane. Each pane
keeps its own conversation and composer.

Two work surfaces can remain visible together. Drag
Memory, Browser or Library from the navigation rail to either workspace
edge, or choose **Open Beside** from its right-click menu. Artifact rows can be dragged
the same way. At two panes, opening another surface replaces the focused pane so
each remains readable. Studio restores the saved arrangement on the next launch.

To replace what a pane shows, drag a navigation item, a place from the Space's
sidebar or **New chat** onto the middle of that pane: it lights up, and lets go
puts the item there, with what the pane showed parked behind it. A pane you pinned
gives way too, since you chose it, and its pin is released. A destination already
shown alone in the other pane trades places with the pane you drop it on. Only the
outer strip of each side opens a new pane beside. Inside a notebook, the item opens
in the notebook's chat or document slot you drop it on.

With more than one Studio window open, **New chat**, an opened chat, and a
reader selection sent to Chat land in the window you clicked in. When that
window cannot show Chat — every pane there is pinned with Chat parked behind
one, or the click came from a popped-out Reader — the chat opens in the other
window and a banner in the window you clicked in reads **Opened in the other
ForeverLM window** (or "another" when more than one other is open). A
selection's confirmation says the same in one line.

Your day is the Mac's Calendar. At the foot of the navigation rail, over your account, a calendar glyph is always there, with a dot on its corner while something is happening: the event the clock is in, an event starting within 15 minutes, or the bout you are in. In the toolbar of a pop-out Reader the **Now** chip says the same in words, with how long the event has left and a hairline along its foot showing how far through it the clock is; in a quiet hour the chip is not there. The **Today** menu in the menu bar has the day's commands at any hour. Click the glyph (or the chip) for today's events: the one you are in highlighted, a line at the time between events, what is behind in grey, and the day's all-day events on one line. A row opens its event in the Calendar app. The event you are in offers its call link when it has one (**Join Zoom**, **Join Teams**, **Join Google Meet**, …), **Start Pomodoro Timer…**, which asks what the session is for and how many minutes it runs (what is left of the event to begin with, or 15, 25, 45, 60 or 90 in a click) before the clock starts, and **Open in Calendar**; a block an assistant planned for a notebook adds **Open Notebook**, and a block that names only sources adds **Make Notebook from This Block**, a notebook titled as the block with those sources. It reads the calendars you choose in **Plugins → Calendar**, which turns the Mac's Calendar on and picks which calendar new events go to. A Google, Exchange or subscribed calendar is part of your day once the Mac's Calendar holds it; see [Plugins](/external-plugins#calendar).

An assistant plans the day by adding events to your calendar. Type `/plan` in a chat (`/plan tomorrow` for the next day; from 2 PM on, `/plan` plans tomorrow), choose **Plan the Day in Chat** from the **Today** menu (⌘D) or the calendar glyph, or ask Claude or ChatGPT with the ForeverLM plugin. The assistant reads the day and how your last few days went, asks one question — what is fixed, and what the day is for — and proposes the blocks. When you agree, it adds each one as an event in the free time the calendar leaves, with what the hour is for in its notes. Meetings with other people stay where they are: ForeverLM never changes an event with other people on it. `/today` says what is on the calendar right now. Each morning whose calendar holds nothing you planned (meetings with other people and recurring events do not count), a **Plan your day?** card waits at the bottom left of the window, with a notification once if ForeverLM is not in front. Switch it off in **Settings → General → Day**, where **Day starts at** and **and ends at** set the hours of your day. Turn on **Make me plan** there to be made to: on such a morning the planning chat opens by itself the first time you are at your Mac, and the card has no close button and cannot be hidden, until your calendar holds a plan of your own or you switch **Make me plan** off.

**Day**, in the **Today** menu and the last item of the calendar glyph's popover, shows your calendar beside the record the calendar cannot hold: what ForeverLM saw you do on a day, on one clock: a paper read in the Reader, an episode heard, a chat had, a Page written. Delete a sitting there if it did not happen. An assistant reads the same log with `get_day_activity` beside the calendar, to see where a planned day went.

A **learning bout** puts a clock on a stretch of learning. Start one from the calendar glyph, on the event you are in or on its own, or from the **Today** menu (⇧⌘B), and the chip counts it; the bout ends when you write up what you learned and what you still do not understand, and that write-up, never the clock, is what earns the break. A bout past its time keeps running and says how far over it is, because nothing ends it but you. The break is a minute of rest for every nine minutes learned, from five up to twenty, so a ninety-minute bout earns about ten, and it is earned from the minutes actually learned rather than the time you set. Letting a bout go is always allowed and earns nothing. The break counts down on your iPhone too, on the Home screen and in the Today widget, and the phone notifies you when it is over. Claude and ChatGPT can start, end and write up a bout over MCP, because the reflection is usually a conversation rather than a form.

A recurring meeting in your library can be given a schedule: **Schedule…** on the series' sidebar menu sets the weekdays, the start time, the length and the time zone. When a session's transcript arrives, ForeverLM reads the action items out of it — who agreed to do what, by when, as the transcript said — and an assistant lists and ticks them off with `list_meeting_action_items` and `set_meeting_action_item_done`. A Zoom meeting recorded on this Mac is found whether or not Save Captions was on: the watcher reads the recording folders under ~/Documents/Zoom as well as the caption files, files a converted recording as a session of its series, transcribes it, and hands a recording Zoom left unconverted back to Zoom to convert. A call that dropped and was started again is still one meeting: a second session of the same series that began on the same day within four hours of the first is folded into the first as its transcript lands, its text following under a "Reconnected at" line and its files moving with it. Sessions that were split before that get **Merge Same-Day Sessions** on the series' menu (or `merge_meeting_sessions` over MCP).

**Goals** are what you want to be true by a date. They have no tab since 2026-10-10: ask the chat ("what are my goals?") and it lists them with their deadlines, and `/goal` sets one. A Goals list in the Space (**New ▸ Goals List**) keeps the ones you choose in view: its **Add Goals ▾** sets a new goal or brings in one already made. Each goal shows its date, and how long is left only when it is overdue or due within three days, with its notebook as an optional tag. **Move Up** and **Move Down** in a goal's menu put it where you want it; a Goal you placed stays where you put it whatever its deadline does, and **Sort Goals by Deadline** forgets the order you made. Setting a goal is one sentence and a deadline picked from named days; a notebook (**Tag a notebook**) is offered below a divider and never required. A Goal can be for a Page, a Site or an animation: click a goal to open what it is for. Its menu has **Edit Goal…**, **Find Directions**, **Open** what it is for (or **Link a Page or Site…** when it has nothing yet), **Change Deadline…**, **Mark done** or **Archive**, and **Delete…**, which removes it after asking once: the Goal's record, its source pool and its Schedule tags go, the sources stay in your library, and a chat started from the Goal stays in Chats.

**Find directions** turns a Goal into research. It sits in the Goal's editor beside **Chat about it**, in a Goal's or an Idea's menu, and in any chat ("find methods to target rare mitochondrial diseases"). It opens a Deep Research chat that reads the goal's sources, the related papers in your library and your Ideas. The chat searches the literature (PubMed, free) and the web, and saves a handful of **Directions**. Each is one sentence naming an approach and whom it is for, why it is worth a look now, the papers it rests on, the strongest case against it, and the cheapest test. The row then reads *3 directions · 2 new*; click it to read them, open or **Add** each paper, and answer: **Pursue**, or **Set aside** with a reason. The next search reads your answers first and never proposes a direction twice. Claude and ChatGPT can run the same search over the plugin (`find_directions`, `propose_directions`).

The Space lists the Pages and Sites you have made or linked, with a place for each kind in its sidebar: **Pages**, **Sites**, and **Google Drive** for the Google Docs you linked. Pictures, animations, audio overviews, videos, walkthroughs and narrations are listed in their notebook's Studio instead ([The Studio column](#the-studio-column)). **Open Pages Beside** (or **Open Sites Beside**) on a row's right-click menu, or dragging the row to an edge of the window, opens that kind in a pane of its own beside what you are viewing. **New ▸ Link a Google Doc…** takes a Google Docs link (its **Open Google Docs** finds one, and a link you copy there is filled in when you come back), and **Link a Site…** does the same for a Codex site or a Claude artifact. Each Page's and Site's card has a **⋯** with **Rename…** and **Move to Trash**. In My Library the Space and the Pages and Sites panes also list what your teams hold (a Page a teammate wrote, a site saved into a team notebook), each with a small two-person mark naming the team on hover; opening one takes you into that team's library. An **animation** is a moving explanation of how something in a source works, drawn as code that plays, scrubs and toggles conditions, or a rendered video. Ask the chat to animate a mechanism from a paper, use `/animate`, or pick **Animate…** from a source's menu; Claude and Codex can save one into your library through the plugin with `save_animation`. An animation is kept exactly as a Site is, in your library and your own iCloud, and stays linked to the sources it explains, so the paper lists its animations and the animation opens its paper.

Pages in a pane of its own shows your pages as cards, newest first, with **All**, **Published**, **Drafts**, **Archived** and **Hidden** filters, a search field and **New Page**. A new page opens on its title: type a name and press Return, and the caret is in the page (left untitled, the page takes its name from its first `#` heading). Click a card to open the page; the list beside an open page is unchanged. A Google Doc you link with **Link a Google Doc…** is listed under **Google Drive** and opens in Google's editor.

Sites in a pane of its own shows the sites made in ForeverLM and the Codex sites and Claude artifacts you have linked, as cards with **All**, **ForeverLM**, **Claude**, **Codex**, **Archived** and **Hidden** filters, a search field and **Link a Site…**. A Page you publish on foreverlm.com stays in Pages, with its Published badge and address; Sites holds only sites. Paste a `….chatgpt.site` address or a `claude.ai/code/artifact/…` link and that page opens in ForeverLM as itself; ForeverLM keeps a read-only text copy that chat and review can read, and **Unlink** turns that copy into an ordinary page in Pages. Select text in an open Site and **Add to Chat** opens a chat beside it carrying the passage and the Site itself, so the tutor can fix the Site's files in your library; **Copy** puts a prompt for Claude or Codex on the clipboard. Every Page's and Site's ⋯ menu offers **Rename…** and **Open in Other Window**. A site made in ForeverLM lives only in your library: its files sync through your own iCloud, it opens in the Mac app, and a team gets it through the team library. It is never put on the web; for a public link, make the page as a Claude artifact or a Codex site and link it here.
