<!-- Source: docs-site/text-to-speech.md -->

# Text to Speech

Text to Speech lets you listen to articles and other text sources in ForeverLM. It is designed for the moments when reading is awkward but listening works: walks, chores, commutes, or reviewing a source before a review session.

## Start listening

Open a source in the Reader and choose **Listen** from the Reader's **⋯** menu, or right-click inside the Reader and choose **Text to Speech**. While the audio is prepared or plays, its control sits on the Reader's toolbar. ForeverLM extracts the readable text, prepares audio, and shows playback controls at the bottom of the reader. Playback is not tied to the reader: switch to another source, close the reader or move to Chat and the audio keeps going, and a Now Playing bar appears at the bottom of the window with the same controls, so there is always a visible way to pause or stop. Click its title to return to the source, and the bar folds back into the reader. To prepare the complete audio without starting playback, right-click the source in Studio and choose **Generate Audio**.

While a source's audio is being generated, its row in the Library shows a spinner where the speaker badge appears once the audio is ready. While cloud audio is being generated, the progress status names the exact model handling that generation alongside its completion percentage. It remains tied to the in-flight generation even if the model selected in Settings changes before the remaining chunks finish. Web Studio shows the same model and percentage while it generates each chunk.

Sources that already carry their own audio — podcast episodes, YouTube videos, and meeting sessions whose recording plays in the reader — do not offer Text to Speech. Play the original recording instead; generating speech from their transcripts would only duplicate it. Meeting sessions without a playable recording (for example Read AI imports, which are transcript-only) keep Text to Speech.

Playback controls include:

- Pause and resume
- Back 15 seconds
- Forward 15 seconds
- Speed selection from 0.75x to 2x
- Stop

## Text-to-speech models

Choose the Text to Speech model in **Settings** -> **Voice** -> **Text to speech**
on the Mac, or **Settings** -> **Text to Speech** on the iPhone. The list is
every speech model OpenRouter serves
([openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=speech](https://openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=speech)),
read live, so a model OpenRouter adds appears without an app update. The Mac
lists a Suggested model from each maker first, then every model by maker with a
search, each with OpenRouter's price; the selected model's voices and the
default speed follow. While the list is being read the pane says so, and if OpenRouter
cannot be reached it says why and offers **Try Again**, showing the last list
it read.

Every model, Grok and Gemini included, is requested from OpenRouter. Cloud
voices run on your own OpenRouter key, and OpenRouter bills them at its cost
with nothing added. The one exception is Orpheus 3B, which OpenRouter still
lists but ForeverLM leaves out: it resets its intonation every ~180 characters,
so it cannot read anything long.

A model's voices are the ones OpenRouter lists for it. Where ForeverLM knows a
voice, it has a name, an accent flag, and the languages it reads. Other voices
are shown by their id. Fish Audio's models list no voices on OpenRouter, so they
use the voice OpenRouter's own sample for them uses. Seed Audio lists none at
all and speaks in its provider's default voice.
Voice pickers prefix provider-documented regional accents with their country
flag and use `🇺🇳` for multilingual voices, and for voices whose languages are
not published, instead of a generic globe glyph.
The native apps prepare the short “Mitochondria are much more than just the
powerhouse of the cell” sample in the background for the voices ForeverLM
curates (the first voice of a model it does not curate). Every voice of the
selected model gets a separate high-priority, bounded warm-up, so its preview
buttons play from a durable device cache once preparation completes. A sample
ForeverLM has already made comes from its own servers at no cost; only a voice
nobody has sampled yet is a billed request, so any other voice's sample is made
when you tap it.
Thumbs-up and thumbs-down reactions are saved per model and voice and follow the
account across the Mac, iPhone, and Web Studio.

Every narration voice is a cloud voice: the text goes to OpenRouter and the
model's provider. A `:free` model costs nothing. See
[AI Providers & Models](/ai-providers) for the complete model list.

## Sources that are not in English

Every model ForeverLM curates declares which languages it narrates, and
ForeverLM checks a source against that declaration before it generates anything.
OpenRouter publishes no language list, so a model or voice ForeverLM does not
curate has its languages marked as not published. That is never read as English.
Such a model is never picked as a replacement for a language, and a source is
never moved off it; its card says the languages are not published. The check
is on-device and deterministic: it samples several windows spread across the
source — not just the opening, which is often an English title or abstract — and
classifies them. Short, mixed, or ambiguous text is left alone rather than
guessed at.

The default, Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS, is the broadest entry in the catalog: Google
publishes more than 70 languages for it, so most non-English sources are already
covered by the default selection. Most other entries are English-only, and a few
name a short list — MAI Voice 2 ships one voice each for English, Spanish,
French, and German.

When the source is in a language your selection does not narrate, ForeverLM
moves it rather than generating anyway. A sibling voice of the same model wins
first (German text goes to MAI's German voice, at the same price and latency),
then the default model, then a model with a voice built for that language. The
reader tells you which voice it used and which one it replaced. This matters
because a model handed a language it does not speak still returns audio and
still bills for it — the words are simply read with the wrong pronunciation.

Web Studio does not run this check; it narrates with the model and voice you
selected.

## Pricing before generation

Each model's card shows OpenRouter's price in the unit OpenRouter bills that model by: per million characters for most, per million UTF-8 bytes for Fish Audio, per million text and audio tokens for Gemini, per minute of audio for Seed Audio. `:free` models show as free. The prices come from OpenRouter, for the host it routes each model to, and none is written into the app. A model OpenRouter has not priced shows **Price unknown**, never free. Before an uncached source is generated manually, ForeverLM shows its narration length, how long the finished audio runs, and its cost. That is a total for a model billed by the character. For a model billed another way it is the model's own price ("priced at $1 / $20 per 1M tokens"), because a total would have to be guessed. A selected model is never silently replaced by a second paid one. This confirmation is on by default. Selecting **Don't ask again for this model** suppresses it only for that model, across all of the model's voices; choosing another model asks again. On the Mac it has no Settings pane: ask the chat to turn confirmation back on for the selected model (`read_aloud.confirm_cost`). On the iPhone it is **Confirm cost for this model** in **Settings** -> **Text to Speech**.

The estimate uses OpenRouter's price as last read. The exact charge appears in the **Activity** list under the sidebar's OpenRouter button after generation; retries can add cost. Replaying cached audio does not generate or charge for new speech.

## Automatic audio

Text to Speech can prepare audio on its own, chosen per kind of source: **Articles**, **Papers**, **Books**, **Courses**, and **Explainers**, in any combination. Every kind starts off. Podcasts, videos, and meetings with a recording have none: they arrive as audio already, so ForeverLM never narrates their transcripts. A book's switch covers its chapters, and a course's covers its documents.

**Explainers** is its own kind: "always generate audio for explainers". An explainer is saved as an article-typed source, but it never falls under Articles, so narrating every explainer does not mean narrating every article. With it on, an explainer's audio starts the moment the script is written — from **Generate Explainer** in the Reader's **⋯** menu or the source's menu, or from an assistant's `generate_explainer` — with the selected voice and no cost question: asking for it once is the consent. An explainer that arrives from another device is narrated the same way, and rewriting an explainer narrates the new script. Over MCP it is `kind: "explainer"` in `set_automatic_audio_settings`.

There is no Settings pane for it. You set it by asking — in the app's chat, or from Claude or ChatGPT connected over MCP — for example "always generate audio for articles from Martin Picard", "narrate every new paper about mitochondria", or "stop generating audio for books". The assistant calls `set_automatic_audio_settings`, and `get_automatic_audio_settings` tells it what is on, what each kind has waiting, and what that would cost.

Each kind takes an optional natural-language rule. A rule is judged from each source's title, author, journal, year, collection, URL, and short description by the **Automatic Audio Filtering** background task. It is tried against the sources already waiting before it is saved, and the reply lists what matched with the combined characters and price; an invalid or failed AI answer never saves the rule, so it never broadens the queue. An empty rule means every source of that kind.

Switching a kind on starts every matching source already in the library as well as later arrivals. A free voice needs no further permission. A paid voice is refused until the account consents to paid voices, and an assistant is told to put the priced total for the waiting library to you before it passes that consent. A voice with no exact catalog price never runs. The Mac and iPhone workers re-read the voice and the consent between every source, so a withdrawn consent or a changed voice stops the next item rather than the pass as a whole.

The iPhone's **Automatically continue books** setting is separate: it generates the next chapter when the current one finishes, whether or not the Books switch is on.

The switches, rules, and paid consent are all per account and sync, so a kind switched on from any chat behaves the same on the Mac and the iPhone, which do the generating. Automatic speech on a free voice costs nothing; on a consented paid voice every generated source is billed to your OpenRouter key. A non-empty semantic rule also uses the configurable background text model when it is checked or re-evaluated, so that smaller filtering call has an AI cost of its own regardless of which voice is selected.


### Listening to a book

Listening to a book chapter runs on into the next chapter when it ends, so starting chapter one commits to the whole book rather than to that chapter. Text to Speech prices it that way: the confirmation names the book and shows two lines, the chapter you started and the whole book, each with its character count, listening length, and estimated cost. Chapters whose audio is already cached are left out of the book total, since replaying them costs nothing.

Approving that price approves the book. Playback moves from chapter to chapter without asking again. Changing the Text to Speech model or voice still invalidates mismatched cached audio, but a model whose confirmation was dismissed stays dismissed when only its voice changes; choosing another unsuppressed model asks again.

The chapter line is measured from the exact narration text. The rest of the book is estimated from each chapter's stored length before its narration is prepared, so the book total is close rather than exact, and a chapter with no stored text yet is left out instead of guessed at.

Web Studio shows the same two lines when you generate audio for a book chapter there, estimating sibling chapters from their word counts. The iPhone shows the book's price in the confirmation itself, because chapter continuation there generates the next chapter in the background without a second prompt: approving one chapter is approving the book, and the alert says so.

### Generating a whole book

Right-click a book in the Library's **Books** tab and choose **Generate Audiobook** to narrate every chapter that does not have audio yet, in reading order, after one price confirmation for the whole book. A book whose every chapter has audio shows a filled speaker badge on its row; a dimmed speaker with a count means some chapters have it. A panel at the bottom of the sidebar follows the batch: one bar per book with the chapter being narrated, a **Stop** button while anything is still running, and the tally once it finishes, which stays until you dismiss it. Stopping keeps every finished chapter; chunks already generated are cached, so generating those chapters again costs nothing for them.

### Generating from an AI assistant

A connected assistant can do the same through MCP. Ask it to "generate audio for all my books", for one book, or for particular sources, and it calls `generate_source_audio`, which uses the voice chosen in Settings. When the run would cost money the tool answers with an estimate first — characters, listening time, price and model — and starts nothing until the assistant calls again with your explicit agreement; a free voice starts immediately. The same progress panel shows in the app, and the assistant can report progress with `get_source_audio_status` or stop the batch with `cancel_source_audio_generation`. See the [MCP Tools Reference](/mcp-tools#text-to-speech-audio).

### Equations and tables

Text to Speech never recites an equation symbol by symbol. Papers and articles run through a preparation pass before narration that states what an equation expresses when the surrounding text gives enough context and otherwise leaves it out, turns a table into a sentence about what it shows, and drops citation markers. A book or course chapter is read as it stands unless its text carries the layout that pass exists for — displayed equations, LaTeX, or table rows — in which case it gets the same pass, so a textbook chapter is narrated like a paper while a novel's chapter costs no text-model call. Inline chemistry in running prose, such as "CO2 and H2", is read as written.

## Caching

For cloud TTS providers, generated audio can be cached so replaying the same source does not regenerate every chunk. Studio can show a Text to Speech cache indicator for sources with cached audio.

If the source changes or the chosen provider, model, or voice changes, ForeverLM may need to generate fresh audio.

When cloud TTS finishes generating every chunk for a source, ForeverLM uploads the audio with the source to your iCloud, and your other Macs and the iPhone fetch each part when it plays. The iPhone can play that audio immediately. If a paper or article has no audio yet, asking Siri on the iPhone to play it can generate it on demand through managed AI, cache it in the same synced format, and start playback without needing the Mac.

Web Studio offers the models ForeverLM curates and requests each from OpenRouter as well, Grok and Gemini included, through ForeverLM's proxy. It keeps audio generated there in its bounded, signed-in browser cache. It resumes from completed chunks after a failed request and plays the cached audio from the Reader's **Listen** button.

## iPhone voice

### Talk

The iPhone talks with you turn by turn. Where you start it decides what it talks about and where the conversation is saved, exactly as if you had typed it:

- **Talk** in the Reader or on a source row (swipe it), or **Talk It Through** at the end of a walkthrough: a chat about that source, kept in the notebook you opened it in, if any.
- **Talk** in a notebook's Chat tab, or the waveform on its row on Home: a chat about the notebook's ticked sources, kept in the notebook. With a chat open, Talk continues that chat by voice, and so does **Continue chat with voice** in the Reader's chat.
- **Review me** in a notebook's Studio: the same notebook chat, opened with "Quiz me on these sources, one question at a time."
- **Review by Voice** in the **⋯** of the iPhone's card review: today's whole memory review, spoken.
- The waveform button on Home, and CarPlay: ForeverLM first offers a source, the audio you were last playing, else something on today's plan, else what you read or discussed most recently. "Shall I quiz you on …? Say yes, name another source, or ask for your memory review." Say yes, or a title, and it talks about that source; ask for your memory review ("my memory review", "what's due") and it holds today's review instead.

Apple's speech recognition hears you and waits for a short pause. Your chat model answers as it would in a typed chat, and Apple's speech synthesis speaks the answer. In a chat, the model is asked to keep spoken answers short and free of formatting, since they are heard rather than read. The microphone is off while ForeverLM speaks, so let it finish before you answer. The screen shows what it heard or is saying and the sources it reads, with Mute and End. Ending shows the conversation's transcript and takes you back where you started.

### Siri

Siri's ForeverLM shortcuts (**Ask ForeverLM**, **Quiz me with ForeverLM** and the rest) run a hands-free loop that controls listening and source audio:

- Start playing a source by title, position, current source, or best available default
- Pause, resume, or stop playback
- Move forward or backward in the current audio
- Change playback speed between 0.75x and 3x
- Tell you what source is currently active
- List the sources in your synced library
- Generate or reuse TTS and immediately read a paper or article aloud
- Refresh the synced library and its audio

It can also enter source chat and review:

- Start a voice review for the current source or another synced source
- Pause the current TTS audio and prepare the source text for questions
- Treat a spoken question during playback as a request to pause and answer from the current text
- Continue a source-grounded conversation once review mode is active
- End review mode and optionally return to audio playback

Typical flows:

- Ask Siri to have ForeverLM play an article.
- While listening, ask to pause so you can talk about the article. ForeverLM pauses playback, loads the synced source text, and waits for your question.
- Ask any question about the text. The source chat answers from the synced source text and speaks the response aloud.
- Continue asking follow-up questions naturally.
- Ask to go back to listening when you are done reviewing.

Talk and Siri both need Sign in with Apple. Their chats and reviews are saved through the same CloudKit records the Mac ingests.

## Good use cases

Text to Speech pairs especially well with Schedule:

- Listen to today's assigned article
- Pause to make a quick note or ask Chat a question
- Start a review after listening
- Mark the scheduled source complete after the review is linked

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/ai-providers.md -->

# AI Providers & Models

**AI runs on your own OpenRouter API key.** Create one at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys) and add it under **API keys** in the OpenRouter button at the bottom of the sidebar. OpenRouter bills every model at its own cost, and ForeverLM adds nothing on top. OpenRouter is the only supported provider today. **AI is never part of ForeverLM's price**: no credits, no tier, and every model OpenRouter serves. Pay models at cost, or use free models and pay nothing. You pick a provider and model for each AI capability in **Settings**, and the **Activity** list under the sidebar's OpenRouter button shows what each request cost, precise below a cent.

Every text model, whether Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI or the long tail, is served through [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai), on your key, by way of ForeverLM's proxy. A request never falls back silently to another route.

You can also skip the built-in AI entirely and drive ForeverLM from Claude, Codex, Gemini, or Grok, [connected over MCP](/setup-mcp). Connecting an assistant is ForeverLM's one paid part (MCP: 7 days free, then $19 once), and ForeverLM charges nothing per MCP tool call: your assistant's subscription covers the thinking. Sources, Schedule, and semantic search work either way. Most people mix the two.

## Chat and reviews (text models)

In-app Chat and reviews use the Default Model chosen in **Settings → Chat** (or in the **Set up ForeverLM** guide). Until you choose one it is Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5. Background tasks (like paper metadata extraction) run on the two Background models in **Settings → Background**: **Text-only**, and **Multimodal** for the work that looks at a figure or a slide. Any one task can have a model of its own on the **Tasks** tab; until you give it one it follows the Background model of its kind. The chat can change them too (`set_ai_task_settings`).

**Settings → Chat** starts with a **Suggested** list: one model from each maker (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, Meta, NVIDIA and others), the top model that is still affordable, shown as the newest release of its family that OpenRouter lists, so a new release takes its place without an app update. Under it are OpenRouter's **Free** models, then **All models on OpenRouter**: every model OpenRouter serves, as a table you can search and sort, or narrow to free or discounted models. Each column's header has its own filter behind a funnel: the Model column by what a model can do or whether it is new, Maker by maker, Price by price band, Context and Speed by a minimum, Provider by whether you chose one. Models OpenRouter listed in the past week are marked **New**, and the refresh button beside the title reads OpenRouter's list again and says which models are new. A row's check offers the model in the chat's model picker, and its menu makes it the Default Model or a backup. **Settings → Background** lists its models the same way, a price tier down.

Notes:

- The long-tail models (DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, GLM, GPT OSS, Mistral, Llama, and Nemotron) are served through OpenRouter like every other text model. The picker groups them by the lab that trained them, and you can add any other compatible model from OpenRouter's directory.
- DeepSeek and Kimi are offered only through OpenRouter's US-routed inference; the labs' own APIs are deliberately not integrated.
- **Don't show models that train on my data** (Settings → Data & Privacy; Settings on iPhone) takes the models that train on what you send them out of every model picker, and routes every OpenRouter request only to hosts that neither retain prompts nor train on them, using OpenRouter's `data_collection: deny` provider preference. One model is priced for training: Meta's Muse Spark 1.2 Contributor, whose discount is paid in training consent. The app does not label it; the switch hides it. A model with no compliant host is refused with a message that names the switch. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google's paid API and xAI do not train on API traffic under their own terms, which the switch does not change.
- A model is admitted only while OpenRouter publishes its price, and every charge is the cost OpenRouter reports for that request. A model it cannot price is refused instead of being estimated.
- **Speed, priced per tier.** On the OpenRouter route the chat composer's model menu offers **Speed: Standard / Fast** for a model whose lab publishes a fast-processing endpoint on OpenRouter (`openai/fast`, `anthropic/fast`). Each speed is listed with its own input / output price from that endpoint — Fast is typically double — and a Fast request names the endpoint explicitly with fallbacks off, so it is never quietly served at another tier; OpenRouter's receipt for the endpoint that ran is the cost recorded. A Standard request names no endpoint, so when the lab's endpoint refuses it (a 429 from Google AI Studio, say) OpenRouter moves it to the same model's other standard endpoint rather than failing the chat; tier endpoints are never part of that fallback. A bolt on the model chip shows Fast is on. Models with no fast endpoint show no speed control.
- **Promotions are named, not applied twice.** When OpenRouter is running a promotion on a model's endpoint, the price in the composer menu already reflects it and the subtitle says so ("$2 in / $10 out · 50% off"). Settings → Chat shows the same label on the model's row.
- The chat's model picker shows only the models you offer; turn off the ones you never use in **Settings → Chat**.
- Each provider remembers its own model choice, so switching providers doesn't reset your selection.

## Text to Speech (text-to-speech)

[Text to Speech](/text-to-speech) offers every speech model OpenRouter serves ([openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=speech](https://openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=speech)). The Mac and the iPhone read that list live, so a model OpenRouter adds appears without an app update, with the voices OpenRouter lists for it. Every request goes to OpenRouter, Grok and Gemini included. It goes straight to OpenRouter on your key, or through ForeverLM's proxy on a leftover balance. Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS with Kore remains the default, and it is also the widest-reaching entry: Google publishes more than 70 languages for it, from Afrikaans and Arabic through Mandarin, Swahili, Tamil, and Vietnamese. The models ForeverLM curates declare their languages. Others are marked as not published, never assumed to be English. Orpheus 3B is left out because it resets its intonation every ~180 characters.

Each model shows OpenRouter's price in the unit OpenRouter bills it by, for the host it routes the model to. Most are per million characters, Fish Audio per million UTF-8 bytes, Gemini per million text and audio tokens, and Seed Audio per minute of audio. The free `:free` models show as free. None of these prices is written into the app, and a model OpenRouter has not priced shows **Price unknown**. The free routes have no production latency or availability guarantee. The exact cost OpenRouter reports, rather than the picker's price, is the record.

On-device macOS speech and a local Qwen3-TTS server remain available without cloud inference cost.

## Voice input (speech-to-text)

Voice dictation in Chat on the Mac uses the model chosen in **Settings → Voice → Speech to text**. The recording is transcribed after you stop, by any transcription model OpenRouter serves ([openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=transcription](https://openrouter.ai/models?output_modalities=transcription)). The list is read live and grouped by maker, and GPT-4o mini Transcribe is the default. Meeting recordings and podcast episodes use the same list (`speech_to_text.recordings_model`, set from the chat). Each model shows OpenRouter's price per hour of audio, or per million tokens for a model billed by tokens (the GPT-4o transcribe models, Gemini 3.5 Transcribe). Every transcription request goes to OpenRouter.

Audio is sent only to the model you chose, through OpenRouter, and is not kept after transcription. The web library's composer dictates on the same model, through ForeverLM's proxy, once you stop recording.

On the iPhone, the composer's microphone and voice conversations use Apple's on-device speech recognition. It is free, works offline, and is not a model you pick.

## Semantic search

Semantic source search runs entirely on-device using Apple's NaturalLanguage contextual embeddings. It costs nothing and sends nothing over the network.

## Costs

- **Your key pays, at OpenRouter's cost.** With an OpenRouter key stored under **API keys** in the OpenRouter button at the bottom of the sidebar, everything ForeverLM sends through OpenRouter goes on your key and OpenRouter bills you directly. ForeverLM adds nothing to it. The key covers text models (chat, reviews, and background tasks) *and* every voice, speech-to-text, image and video model OpenRouter serves: the Gemini and Grok voices, GPT-4o mini transcription, the GPT Image, Gemini, FLUX, Recraft and Seedream image models, and Veo, Kling, Wan, Sora and the other video models. **Settings → AI Models → Images** and **→ Videos** list every one of them, read from OpenRouter each time the pane opens, so a model OpenRouter adds shows up there on its own; each card shows OpenRouter's price. Over MCP the same setting is `get_own_router_key` / `set_own_router_key`.
- **Your key never touches ForeverLM's servers.** It is saved only in your Keychain, which iCloud Keychain syncs end-to-end encrypted to your Macs and iPhone, and the app sends it only to OpenRouter. Connect OpenRouter signs in at openrouter.ai and hands the key back to the app on your Mac directly. The remote ForeverLM connector refuses to carry a key, so an AI assistant cannot set one through it; paste the key into the app instead.
- **The app's price is separate from AI.** ForeverLM itself is free. MCP, the connection for an outside assistant, is 7 days free from your first sign-in, then $19 paid once (no subscription), before applicable tax, in **Settings → Billing**. Paying never buys AI: your key runs every model, and OpenRouter's free models cost nothing.
- The **Activity** list under the sidebar's OpenRouter button itemises every request with the exact cost OpenRouter reports, precise below a cent. Models without a published rate are shown as unpriced rather than guessed.
- **Prepaid balance is retired.** ForeverLM no longer sells AI balance or offers auto top-up. A balance left from an earlier purchase is shown, read-only, while it lasts, and pays for requests sent without your own key. While a key is stored, it pays for nothing.
- Background tasks (paper metadata extraction, transcript cleanup, search embeddings) run on the same key and are itemised per task in the ledger. They run on the Background models in **Settings → Background**, which the chat can change too (`set_ai_task_settings`), so a cheap or free model there keeps them cheap. While the Text model is free, meeting work stays on a paid model unless you let it use the free one: a meeting's transcript holds private conversations. Each Background model can also list up to ten **backups**, tried in order when it is busy, fails or sends back nothing usable: right-click a model and choose **Use as Backup**. A backup is billed at its own price. A free model you pick brings the next two free models as its backups when it has none. The chat's model can list backups too, in **Settings → AI Models → Chat**, but only a scheduled task's run moves to them: a chat you type in stays on the model you picked.
- If a provider or model can't complete a request, ForeverLM surfaces the error — it never falls back to a model that is not one of the setting's listed backups, or to heuristic grading.

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/articles.md -->

# Articles

ForeverLM automatically surfaces articles you've saved to your browser's reading list, making them available for AI-assisted learning via MCP.

## Supported Browsers

Reading list sync works with **Safari**, **Google Chrome**, and **Brave**. The app discovers saved articles from all three browsers automatically on macOS.

## How Articles Are Discovered

**Safari Reading List (automatic):**
The app reads the Reading List in `~/Library/Safari/Bookmarks.plist` and adds new items to your queue automatically. macOS protects that file, so if the scan is blocked, add ForeverLM in **System Settings** → **Privacy & Security** → **Full Disk Access** (use the **+** button; macOS does not list it until you do), turn it on, and relaunch the app.

**Chrome & Brave Reading List (automatic):**
The app reads reading list entries from Chrome and Brave's local data. No special permissions are needed. Just add articles to your reading list in either browser and they'll appear under **Articles** in the Library.

**Choosing browsers and how far back to go:**
Setup's Articles step asks one question, which browser you use: Safari, Chrome, Brave, or several. The Mac's default browser is marked Recommended. Pages saved in the last 30 days come in first, and everything you save after that arrives on its own. Every page that comes in is fetched and cleaned up by AI once, so a long backlog costs more. Change the browsers, or how much of what is already saved to bring in (**Everything**, the **Last 30 days**, or **Only new saves**), in **Settings → Sources → Reading Lists**, or from chat (`sources.reading_list_browsers` and `sources.reading_list_import_window`). A wider choice imports the pages it now reaches right away.

**Via MCP:**
Your AI assistant can add articles using the `add_source` tool.

**From a read-later app:**
A one-time import, described [below](#coming-from-a-read-later-app).

## Coming from a Read-Later App

If your saved articles live in Readwise Reader, Instapaper, Raindrop, Pocket, Omnivore or a similar app, bring them over once. Setup's Articles step has **Coming from Readwise, Instapaper or Pocket?**, which opens a page with **Choose Export…**. Choose the file the app exported, or the unzipped export folder:

- **Readwise Reader:** Settings → Export, then the CSV.
- **Instapaper:** Settings → Export, then the CSV or HTML file.
- **Raindrop:** Settings → Backups, then the CSV or HTML file.
- **Pocket, Omnivore and others:** the export you downloaded, as a file or an unzipped folder.

ForeverLM reads any CSV with a link column, any bookmarks HTML file (the format browsers export), JSON exports whose records carry a link, and plain lists of links. Each link becomes an article with its title, the date you saved it, and whether you had archived it; the full text is then fetched in the background, one article at a time. Links already in your library are not added twice, and items a reader only showed you from a feed, which you never saved, are left out. It is a one-time copy: nothing keeps syncing with the other app afterwards, and it is never changed.

## Using Articles with AI

Once an article appears in Studio:

1. **Select** the article. The app fetches and displays the full text.
2. The content is now available to your AI assistant via MCP.
3. Ask your AI to explain key concepts, quiz you on the material, or compare it with other sources.

## When a Publisher Blocks the Fetch

Some sites answer ForeverLM's background fetch with a bot check instead of the article, and the row then reads **Blocked by a publisher security check**. Nothing from the check is stored, so the article is not silently replaced by a few lines of boilerplate.

Open the article anyway. The reader is a real browser session, so the check usually clears there and the page loads. Once it has, ForeverLM saves that page as the article: the text becomes the source's content, the HTML is archived for offline reading, and the row stops showing the block. The background fetch also waits a few seconds for a check that clears on its own before giving up, so many of these never reach the row at all.

## Tips

- Articles with dense, mechanism-heavy content (research blogs, technical deep-dives) work best for explain-it-back learning.
- Use semantic search to find articles related to a concept across your library.

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/books.md -->

# Books

ForeverLM treats books differently from articles and papers. Each chapter of a book is a source of its own, so you read, listen to and review a book a chapter at a time.

## Adding a Book

On the Library's **Books** tab, choose **Add Book…**, or drop the file on the tab: a PDF, an EPUB, or a DRM-free Kindle book. ForeverLM copies it into your library, which syncs it through your iCloud, and the book is there to read at once. A PDF book opens as the whole book, with its own outline as the Contents, and an EPUB opens as the whole book in reading order, while their chapters are found in the background; a small spinner on the book's row says what it is doing. Your **Book Chapter Splitting** model (on the **Tasks** tab of **Settings → Background**) finds them: for a PDF it reads the outline, and each chapter is a run of the PDF's pages; for an EPUB it groups the book's own documents into chapters. Either way the book stays one file, with nothing unpacked beside it. When the chapters arrive, anything you marked and the place you reached move to the chapter they belong to, and a book open in the Reader follows you there. If the chapters can't be found, ForeverLM says so and tries again the next time it opens, and the book stays readable as one piece. Your **Book Author** model also reads the front matter for a better title and author, and a file that reads like a scholarly paper is pointed out rather than split. An assistant connected over MCP can send an EPUB with `import_epub`.

A book is the same book only when it is the same file. Adding a file you added before keeps the one book, even after ForeverLM wrote a scan's text or an EPUB's chapters into its copy. A different file is a different book, whatever its title: a textbook and a 1957 monograph both called *Bioenergetics* are two books, each in a folder of its own (the second one's name gets the start of a code that identifies its file, such as `Bioenergetics 4545308b`), and adding one never changes the other's details, chapters or file. Two books may share a title, and renaming a book to another one's title is fine. To give a book a fresh copy of its file, such as a clean download of a damaged EPUB, right-click the book and choose **Replace Book File…**; its chapters are found again in the new file.

Older builds kept a PDF book as one file per chapter, and an EPUB unpacked into a folder of its files. The first launch of a build that keeps every book as one file puts each such book back together: a PDF book as its own PDF where every chapter's pages are still in it, or else the chapters joined; an EPUB by packing its folder back into the book's file. Nothing about a chapter changes, its highlights and reading position included.

A scanned PDF, whose pages are only pictures, is read in the background before its chapters are found. A book counts as scanned when at least half its pages carry no text of their own; an ebook or a publisher's PDF never does, even with a picture cover or photo pages. On the Mac, OCR reads every page of a scan that carries no text of its own. Your **Scanned Page Proofreading** model, also on the **Tasks** tab, then checks each page's lines against a picture of the page and corrects what OCR misread, such as K⁺, β or 10⁻⁷. The corrected text is written into the book's PDF beneath the print, so chapters, search and highlights all work as they do in a book that came with text. A long scan takes a few minutes, and its proofreading is billed like other background work; you read the pages meanwhile. If proofreading fails, no unchecked text is kept and the book is tried again later.

**Why one source per chapter:**
- Your AI assistant gets more focused context when the source covers one topic
- You can work through chapters as you read, rather than the whole book upfront

## Reading a Book

A book opens at the chapter you pick, where you left it, and reads as one book: scroll past the end of a chapter and the next one follows; scroll up past its start and you are in the one before. On the Mac this holds for a book imported from a PDF and one imported from an EPUB, and a PDF book shows its front matter and index too; on iPhone and iPad it holds for an EPUB book, while a PDF book's chapters open one at a time.

- The Reader's title and position ("6 of 31") follow the chapter you are in, and so does everything that belongs to a chapter: its reading position, how far you got, notes and highlights you make, and the chat you start about a passage.
- **Contents** lists every chapter and jumps to the one you choose: on the Mac choose **Contents…** from the Reader's **⋯** menu, on iPhone and iPad tap the list button in the Reader's toolbar.
- On the Mac, Find searches the whole book. A link inside the book — the contents page, an endnote and its way back — scrolls to what it names.
- On iPhone and iPad the chapters come from iCloud as you reach them, so the next one may take a moment to appear the first time.

## Hiding or Removing a Book

Select a book in the Books list and press Delete, or right-click its cover, then choose **Hide Book**. Every chapter leaves the list together; nothing is deleted, and hiding is visual only, so chat, search and reviews still draw on the book. The foot of the Books list then shows a quiet **N hidden books** row, which opens Hidden Items. Click a hidden book there to read it in the Reader, where it opens like any book, at the chapter you reached; it stays hidden from the Books list. The arrow beside it lists its chapters, and each opens the same way. **Unhide** brings the whole book back, and **Show** one chapter. Selecting several covers and pressing Delete offers **Hide N Books**.

The same confirmation offers **Remove Book from Library**, which forgets the book but leaves its files in iCloud, with a short undo. To delete the files as well, use **Remove Book** in the cover's right-click menu and choose **Remove & Delete Files**.

## Tips

- **Skip appendices and references:** Work through only the chapters you're actively reading.

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/courses.md -->

# Courses

A course in ForeverLM is a path through related sources: lecture videos, papers, book chapters and your own lecture PDFs, with a quiz after each lecture. The sources stay in your library under their own types, so a lecture video is also listed under **YouTube** and a paper under **Papers**; the course lays them out in order.

## Courses and their notebooks

A course is its own thing, not part of a notebook. Every course is in the Space, in its **All** list beside your notebooks and pages and under **Courses** in its sidebar, as a card: its cover, where it comes from, and how far you are. Click a card to open the course's page, laid out the way Khan Academy lays out a unit:

- A card per lecture, with its video, its assigned reading, any notes, slides or problem sets, and its quiz.
- A checkpoint quiz every few lectures, and a course test at the end.
- At the top, your progress and **Continue**, which opens whatever is next.

Everything you have finished carries the same green check: a lecture you watched, a reading you read, a quiz you passed. Finished rows are drawn a little lighter, and the next thing to do is highlighted.

A notebook can follow a course: its sources, and every lecture the course gains later, join the notebook, and the course's page can open beside the notebook's chat. **⋯ › Link to Notebook** makes a notebook you already have follow the course, **⋯ › Make Study Notebook** makes a new one named after it that holds its sources, and **Unlink from** stops one following (it keeps the sources it holds). The page says "Linked to" the notebooks that follow it, under its title. Deleting or merging a notebook never changes a course.

Click a lecture or reading to open it in the Reader beside the course, so the path stays in view while you watch. Right-click a row for more: **Show in Sources**, **Write Quiz** on a lecture, the papers a lecture only cites under **Papers**, and **Remove from Course**. The course's own actions are in the **⋯** menu at the top of its page, or in its card's right-click menu. **Hide Course** takes a course off the list; **Undo** in the notice that follows brings it back, and so can an assistant connected over MCP (`set_group_hidden`).

### Finish a quiz to go on

A quiz holds back what comes after it until you finish it: once every question is answered or skipped, what follows opens, whatever the score. The score still says how you did: three in four questions right (all three in a three-question quiz) is a pass, and you can answer a missed question again in the quiz's chat to raise it. A question you skip counts as not right. Lectures after a quiz you haven't finished show a lock, and when a video would play the next lecture by itself, it stops and offers the quiz instead. Anything you've already watched or read stays open. If a quiz shouldn't stand in the way, rewrite it, or remove it from its menu.

### Sharing a course

To let someone else take a course, share it with a [team](/teams) you are both in: **⋯ › Share with Team ▸** on the course's page or card. The team gets its own copy of the whole course — lectures, readings, material, quizzes and the sources behind them, files included — and every member finds it under the Space's **Courses** with a team mark. Each takes it at their own pace: their own checks, their own quiz passes, and the same locks. Your progress stays yours, and the team's copy starts at the beginning. Share it again after you change the course to bring the team's copy up to date. A team's courses are taken on the Mac; the iPhone shows only My Library.

### On iPhone

Under **Courses** on the home screen, or in **Sources › Courses**, tap a course to open the same page: your progress and **Continue** at the top, then each lecture with its video, readings and quiz, and the checkpoints and course test between them. The same checks and locks show, and tapping a locked row tells you which quiz opens it. Tap a quiz to take it: answer each question in your own words, typed or dictated, and each answer is checked on your chat model before the next. **Skip** at the top moves on without answering. A pass on your iPhone opens what follows on your Mac too, and the other way round. A quiz you leave halfway starts again from the first question.

## Building a course

A course begins in one of three ways: **New Course ▸ From YouTube Playlist…** at the top of the Courses list makes a lecture of each video in a playlist, **New Course ▸ Plan with Chat…** plans one with you ([Generating a course](#generating-a-course)), and a Teachable course comes in whole ([Importing a Teachable course](#importing-a-teachable-course)).

The rest comes from your library. Add lecture slides, problem sets and reading PDFs to ForeverLM like any other file, then drag each onto the course's card or page, or use **Course ▸** in its right-click menu. **Lectures ▸ Add Lecture** in the course's **⋯** menu adds a lecture, **Lectures ▸ Add YouTube Playlist…** adds a playlist's videos to a course you already have, and **Refresh Playlist** brings in what the playlist gained since. A book is read along with the course ([Reading a textbook along with a course](#reading-a-textbook-along-with-a-course)).

Then select course sources and ask Chat, or your AI assistant, to:
- Explain key concepts from the lecture
- Quiz you on the material by explaining it back
- Compare ideas across multiple lectures
- Help you work through problem sets

## Importing from Canvas LMS

If your university uses [Canvas LMS](https://www.instructure.com/canvas), you can bulk-download all course materials using Claude Computer Use and add them to your course.

1. Start a Computer Use session and navigate to your Canvas course
2. Ask Claude to download all lecture slides and readings
3. Add the files to ForeverLM and drag them onto the course

## Adding Video Content

For lecture videos, the workflow depends on the source:

**YouTube lectures:**
Make the course from the playlist, or add the playlist to the course, as above. ForeverLM fetches each lecture's transcript, and the video is listed under **YouTube** too.

**Apple Podcasts lecture series:**
If the course is published as a podcast, add it in Apple Podcasts, listen to each episode, and click **Show Transcript** once per episode. ForeverLM picks up the cached transcript automatically.

### Lecture titles

A playlist's videos are often named for where they sit in a series ("Mitochondrial Cell Biology 2") rather than for what they teach. After a YouTube playlist import, ForeverLM reads each new lecture's transcript and names the lecture for its subject, keeping the video's own title when it already says what the lecture covers. The video row under each lecture still shows the video's title. To rename a course's lectures later, choose **Lectures ▸ Retitle Lectures from Content** in the course's ⋯ menu; it fetches any missing transcripts first. A lecture with no transcript keeps its title, and refreshing the playlist never undoes a title. The model is the **Lecture Titles** task.

## Importing a Teachable course

Courses sold on [Teachable](https://teachable.com), such as conference recordings, come in with their transcripts.

1. Open ForeverLM's browser, choose the **Library** profile, and sign in to the school. Signing in to your own web browser doesn't count, because ForeverLM reads the school with the sign-in made inside the app.
2. Paste any lecture's link (`…/courses/<course>/lectures/<number>`) into a notebook's **Add sources** to add that lecture as a video. To import the whole course, ask your AI assistant to run `import_teachable_course` with the link.

ForeverLM reads the course outline from the lecture page. Each lecture with a video becomes a video on its own lecture, in the school's order. Lectures with only text, such as a CME form, are skipped.

These videos have no captions, so the transcript is made from the audio with speech-to-text. That takes a few minutes per lecture. Each transcript starts with the lecture's own text, such as the talk title and speakers.

Videos on Teachable's own hosting are supported. A school that still uses Wistia gets an error that names it.

## Generating a course

Choose **New Course ▸ Plan with Chat…** at the top of the Courses list, or type `/course <topic>` in any chat. A chat opens with "I want to make a course about " ready for you to finish. It searches your library and, if you agree, the web. Then it proposes modules with their sources and suggested videos, and revises them with you until you're happy. It builds the course only when you say so. If you agree to a video for a module, ForeverLM asks the price in its own dialog first, and the finished film sits under that module as its video.

A generated course is an ordinary course: its modules are its lectures, and **Quizzes ▸ Write Quizzes** in the course's **⋯** menu writes its quizzes.

## Reading a textbook along with a course

Choose **Lectures ▸ Add Textbook…** in a course's **⋯** menu, or drop a book from your library onto the course's card or page. Pick the book and say where you're coming from in **About you**. ForeverLM places the sections of the book worth reading for you after each lecture, with their pages and, on hover, why, and leaves out what your background already covers. Click a reading to open the chapter at its first page. See [Readings from a textbook](/studio#readings-from-a-textbook).

A lecture's quiz asks about its readings too, after the video's questions, each naming its page; a quiz written before you added the book picks them up with **Rewrite Quiz**. The quiz also knows the readings: when you miss a question, the reply links the reading that explains it next to **Rewatch**, and the last grade names the reading most worth doing. Ask it to summarize a lecture's reading and it reads exactly the planned pages.

## Tips

- **Add a whole course to a notebook:** Drag the course's card onto the notebook's row in the rail or its row in the Space. Every lecture and material is added in course order, and anything added to the course later follows into the notebook. The notebook then follows the course.
- **Add a source to a course:** Drag it from Sources onto the course's card or page, or use **Course ▸** in its right-click menu. A source that is on a course offers **Show in Course**.
- **Lecture notes > slides:** Notes usually contain more prose and context than slides alone.
- **Process lecture by lecture** as you watch, so the material is fresh.
- **Problem sets:** Add problem set PDFs too — your AI assistant can help you reason through approaches.

---

<!-- Source: docs-site/papers.md -->

# Papers

Academic papers (from arxiv, Nature, Science, bioRxiv, and similar journals) get special treatment in ForeverLM. Save a paper to your Safari, Chrome, or Brave reading list and the app picks it up automatically, detecting it as a paper by URL and fetching the full PDF whenever possible.

## How Papers Are Detected

ForeverLM classifies a source as a paper in two steps:

**Step 1 — URL detection.** The URL is checked against known academic domains:

- arxiv.org, nature.com, science.org, cell.com
- biorxiv.org, medrxiv.org, plos.org
- pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
- and other major journal publishers

**Step 2 — LLM classification.** Journals like Science and Nature publish both research papers and shorter editorial content (news articles, commentary, perspectives). These live on the same domain, so URL detection alone can't tell them apart. Before downloading a PDF, ForeverLM sends the URL and title to a lightweight LLM call on your Background text model (the **Source Classification** task in **Settings → Background → Tasks**) that classifies the source as a paper or article. Editorial content is automatically moved to the Articles tab.

This also works in the other direction: if a web article turns out to be an academic paper (e.g., a preprint hosted on a personal blog), the LLM reclassifies it after fetching the content.

## Adding a Paper

**From your reading list:**
Save the paper's abstract or landing page to your browser's reading list (Safari, Chrome, or Brave). The app picks it up automatically, as far back as you chose in setup or in **Settings → Sources → Reading Lists** (see [Articles](/articles#how-articles-are-discovered)).

**Manual paste:**
In a notebook, paste the paper's URL or DOI into **Add sources** and choose **Add link**: the paper joins your library and the notebook in one step. In ForeverLM's Browser, **Add to Sources** saves the page you are reading.

**Via MCP:**
Your AI assistant adds a paper with `import_paper_from_url` (a URL or DOI) or `import_local_pdf_as_paper` (a PDF on your Mac). Either way the paper shows in Papers as soon as its PDF is in, as processing until its metadata is read. `add_source` is for non-paper sources. Given a notebook's `notebook_id`, `import_paper_from_url` files the paper in that notebook as well, and a paper already in your library joins it instead of being imported again.

**From Zotero, Paperpile, Mendeley or another reference manager:**
A one-time import, described [below](#coming-from-a-reference-manager).

**From Chat:**
When the [in-app Chat](/in-app-chat#web-search) brings up a paper your library does not hold, it offers to add it. Ask, and it finds the DOI or publisher page itself and imports the paper through the same pipeline as a pasted URL.

## Coming from a Reference Manager

ForeverLM does not connect to Zotero, Paperpile or Mendeley, and that is a decision rather than a gap. Everything the app does with a paper depends on the paper itself living in your library: the PDF sits in your iCloud container, so its text is extracted and searchable, Chat can quote it, Text to Speech can narrate it on your Mac and iPhone, a review can test you on it, and it syncs to every device. A plugin that pointed at a record in another database would enable none of that. It would give you a list of titles and a lock screen.

So instead of a live plugin there is a one-time move. Bring the papers over once and they are ForeverLM papers from then on. Your reference manager keeps doing what it is good at, citations and bibliographies, and is never modified.

**In setup.** The Papers step asks where your papers live: **Zotero**, **Another reference manager**, **PDFs on this Mac**, or **I don't have any yet**, and each answer opens a page with one way in. Zotero is offered only when it keeps its library on this Mac (in `~/Zotero`, or wherever Zotero's settings moved it); its page says how many papers it holds and how many have a PDF, and **Import from Zotero** brings them over in one click. For any other reference manager, **Choose Export…** on its page takes any of these, or several at once:

- **Zotero:** the Zotero folder in your home folder, the one holding `zotero.sqlite` and `storage/` (Zotero → Settings → Advanced → Files and Folders shows where it is). Zotero can stay open.
- **Paperpile:** export BibTeX into the `Paperpile` folder that Paperpile syncs to Google Drive, then choose that folder, so the export's file paths resolve to the PDFs in `All Papers`.
- **Mendeley:** export your library as BibTeX and choose the file. Mendeley Reference Manager's export carries no PDFs, so those papers are added by DOI and the normal PDF fetch completes them.
- **EndNote, JabRef, ReadCube and others:** a BibTeX or RIS export, or a folder of PDFs.

ForeverLM reads the library read-only, copies each PDF into the synced Papers folder, and adds papers that have no PDF by DOI so the normal PDF fetch can try to complete them. A paper already in your library is matched by DOI or title and is not added twice; missing authors or journal are filled in from the export. The metadata and cleanup models then work through the new papers in the background as they do for any other paper.

**Highlights and notes come too.** The highlights, underlines and comments you made in Zotero's reader are brought over with each paper, in their colors, and so are its notes pinned to the page. For any other app, ForeverLM reads the highlights and notes saved inside the PDF file itself. That covers PDFs marked up in Preview or Acrobat, and a PDF your reference manager saved or exported with its annotations. A reference manager that keeps annotations only in its own database or in the cloud leaves them out of the file, and ForeverLM cannot see them there. This works for any PDF you add, not only in a library import: drop an annotated PDF into Papers and its marks arrive with it.

Each one becomes an ordinary ForeverLM highlight. It shows in the reader and the notes list, you can search it, a review takes its note into account, and it syncs to your other devices. A note pinned beside the text is attached to the nearest line, and each color becomes the nearest of ForeverLM's five markers. Importing the same library or PDF again adds nothing twice, and a passage you have already highlighted in ForeverLM keeps your mark. Nothing is written back to the other app or the original file.

**With an AI assistant.** The [ForeverLM plugin](/setup-mcp#claude-code-plugin) includes a paper-library-migration skill: ask Claude Code, or another assistant that has the plugin, to move your reference library into ForeverLM. It reads the reference manager on your Mac, imports each paper through the same pipeline, and reports what landed, what was already there, and what it skipped. The Mac app must be running, because the import happens on your Mac.

## Following a Paper's References

A paper's reference list is the reading list its authors wrote for you. When a paper is open in the reader, choose **Find Cited Papers** from the reader's **⋯** menu (a paper's context menu in the sidebar offers it too). ForeverLM reads the reference list off the paper's PDF, looks each entry up in Crossref and OpenAlex, and lists the papers it found in the same panel: **Add to Library** imports one through the normal paper pipeline, so it gets a PDF, metadata, and cleanup like any other paper, and **Dismiss** waves it off. Papers you already have are marked as such rather than offered again, and an entry that could not be matched to a record is shown as unmatched so you can search for it by hand. Decisions persist and sync, so a paper dismissed on one Mac stays dismissed on the other, and a dismissed paper can be restored from the panel's Dismissed section.

Nothing is read until you ask. Reading the list is a background AI call per stretch of references plus a free catalog lookup per entry, with at most eight paid web searches for entries the catalogs could not place, so a long reference list can take a minute; once it finishes, the menu item becomes **Cited Papers** and says how many are waiting to be added, and opens the panel, whose **Read references again** reads the list once more. The model behind it is the **Paper Reference Extraction** task, on the **Tasks** tab of **Settings → Background**; the chat can change it too (`set_ai_task_settings`).

## How PDF Loading Works

When you add a paper, ForeverLM tries to get the full PDF automatically:

1. **Direct fetch**: downloads the PDF (works for open-access papers on arxiv, bioRxiv, PLOS, etc.)
2. **PubMed Central (PMC)**: fetches the full text if available in PMC

A paper in ForeverLM is a PDF. When every route fails, the paper waits in **Papers that need attention** until a PDF turns up: attach one, or, for a paper you can read on the publisher's site, save it from the page yourself as described below. ForeverLM never reads a publisher's page as the paper on its own.

When a PDF is fetched, it is saved with the paper in your library and syncs through your iCloud to your other devices.

## Dealing with Paywalled Papers

### Open access (no action needed)

Papers on arxiv, bioRxiv, medrxiv, PLOS, and other open-access repositories are fetched automatically.

### PubMed Central (PMC)

If a paper is in PMC (even if the publisher's version is paywalled), ForeverLM detects this and fetches the PMC version automatically.

### Other paywalled publishers

For papers behind paywalls:

1. **Download the PDF** from your institutional access.
2. **Drop it on the paper's row** in Papers, or choose **Attach PDF File…** from the row's right-click menu.

### Read online, but no PDF (Nature and others)

Some subscriptions let you read a paper on the publisher's site but never offer the PDF. Open the paper in ForeverLM: when the publisher refuses the PDF, the reader shows the publisher's page instead of a lock screen. The reader is a real browser session, so sign in to the publisher there if you have not already. Once the page in front of you is the paper, click **Save Paper from Page** in the reader's toolbar (it is in the reader's menu too). ForeverLM stores the page's text as the paper's content, asks the publisher for the PDF once more with your signed-in session, and when the file is still refused prints the page you are reading to a PDF and saves that as the paper's file. The text goes through the same Source Content Cleanup and metadata extraction as a downloaded PDF, so search, chat, review sessions, and Listen work on it, and the reader shows the PDF from then on.

This is your choice each time; ForeverLM never takes a publisher's page for a paper on its own. A page that is the publisher's access wall, or only the abstract and front matter, is refused with a message saying so, so sign in first and make sure the whole paper is on the page.

Signing in matters once, in ForeverLM's reader: your browser's login does not carry over, because the app has its own cookie store. Once you have signed in there, every ForeverLM fetch uses it, including the PDF download, so **Download PDF** in the reader's toolbar may simply get the file, which is the better outcome when the publisher offers one.

Some publishers go further and hand the PDF only to a browser: nature.com, for one, answers any other client with a JavaScript check, whatever cookies it carries. When ForeverLM's own download comes back with a page instead of the file and you have opened that publisher in the reader, the app asks again through the reader's own browser session, in the background, exactly as if you had clicked Download PDF there. The same checks apply as for any downloaded file: it has to be a PDF, a supplementary file such as a Reporting Summary is never taken for the paper, and a paper that already has its PDF is left alone. This is how a paper your subscription covers comes down on its own once you have signed in to the publisher in the reader, and how **Recheck all** on paywalled papers, in the Papers tab or over MCP, recovers it later. A publisher you have never opened in the reader is not tried this way, because there is no session to use.

When an AI assistant runs the bulk PDF download over MCP, papers that fail in a paywall-shaped way (access denied, login or payment required, an HTML page served instead of a PDF, or no open-access copy found anywhere) are automatically marked as paywalled so they stop being retried. Attaching a PDF clears the marker, and the assistant can also clear it with `set_source_paywall_status`.

The same applies when an AI assistant imports a single paper by URL or DOI (`import_paper_from_url`): if the publisher blocks the PDF, the paper is still added, marked paywalled, with the title, authors, venue, year, and DOI the landing page and Crossref provide. It appears in the Papers tab with the paywall recovery options, ready for you to attach the PDF, and a later paywall recheck can pick up a free copy. Only transient failures, such as a network error or a 404, leave nothing behind.

## Tips

- **Search one field only:** the sources search reads a paper's title, authors, journal, year, DOI and address, and also finds papers whose text contains the words. To search titles alone, start the query with `title:` — `title:reverse electron transport` lists only papers with that phrase in the title. `author:`, `journal:`, `year:`, `doi:` and `site:` work the same way, in every sources tab.
- **Preprints are ideal**: arxiv and bioRxiv papers are always freely accessible.
- **Long papers:** the app reads the whole PDF, however long, including methods and resource tables printed after the references.
- **Scanned PDFs:** prefer native PDFs over scans for better text extraction.

<!-- Source: docs-site/journals.md -->

# Feeds

::: warning Feeds is switched off for now
The current app has no Feeds pane in Settings, checks no feeds and offers no suggestions, and the chat has no feed tools. Feeds you already follow stay on your Mac and come back when Feeds does. This page describes how it works when it is on.
:::

Follow the sites you read — journals, blogs, newsletters, preprint listings — and ForeverLM reads their new articles and posts against your notebooks. The ones that fit are offered inside the notebook — you decide whether each becomes a source. Nothing is added to your library until you say so.

## Following a feed

Paste a site's home page or its RSS link to follow it. Any site with an RSS or Atom feed works:

- a Substack or other newsletter — `https://www.astralcodexten.com`
- a Medium publication — `https://netflixtechblog.com`
- a WordPress, Ghost or personal blog — `https://simonwillison.net`
- a preprint listing — `https://rss.arxiv.org/rss/q-bio.SC`
- a journal — `https://www.nature.com/nrm` or `https://www.nature.com/nature.rss`
- a subreddit — `https://www.reddit.com/r/longevity/`

Paste several at once, one per line, and click **Follow**. ForeverLM finds the feed the page advertises, and when a page advertises none it tries the places blogs keep their feed (`/feed`, `/rss`, `/feed.xml`, `/atom.xml`, `/index.xml`), so the home page is almost always enough. If a site hides its feed somewhere unusual, paste the feed link itself.

Each feed is checked about twice a day, and right away when you follow it. Unchanged feeds cost nothing; a feed's row shows when it was last checked and any error the site returned. **Check now** re-fetches every feed.

## Which notebooks are watched

Every active notebook is watched, including one you create later. Nothing to configure.

Each notebook is described to the matching step by what you have written in it: the title, the standing instructions, the research questions, and a sample of the sources already in it. The more precisely the notebook says what it is about, the sharper the suggestions. A notebook about "mitochondrial quality control in ageing muscle" gets the cristae paper and the blog post dissecting a new mitophagy result, not every cell-biology paper or science post of the week.

A blog post is judged on the same terms as a paper: what matters is whether its subject serves the notebook, not what kind of publication it is. Housekeeping — open threads, subscription drives, corrections, tables of contents, link roundups — is not suggested.

## Answering a suggestion

Open the notebook and its **Sources**. New matches wait at the top under **New from your feeds**, each with the site or journal, the date, the title, and one sentence on why it fits. Click the title to read it in your browser.

- **✓ Add** imports the item through the same path a pasted link takes — a paper's PDF is fetched, including through your own publisher login in ForeverLM's reader; a blog post or newsletter issue becomes an article — and adds it to the notebook.
- **✕ Dismiss** removes the suggestion for this notebook. The same item is never offered to that notebook again. Another notebook it matched keeps its own suggestion.

The notebook overview's Sources card shows how many suggestions are waiting.

## Being told

When a check finds matches while ForeverLM is open, a short message appears in the window. To hear about it when ForeverLM is in the background, turn on **Notify me when an article matches**; the banner names the notebook and opens its sources when clicked. It is off unless you turn it on.

## Cost

Matching is one AI call per batch of up to forty new items, paid by your OpenRouter key and listed in the **Activity** list under the sidebar's OpenRouter button as *Feed Article Matching*. Its model follows your Background default, which has no Settings pane; ask the chat to change it (`set_ai_task_settings`).

## What stays on this Mac

Followed feeds and pending suggestions live on the Mac that follows them. An item you add becomes an ordinary source and syncs to every device like any other.
